12.25.oldText: SILVIUS. Phebe, with all my heart.

12.26.oldText: PHEBE. I'll write it straight; The matter's in my head and in my heart; I will be bitter with him and passing short. Go with me, Silvius. Exeunt

12.33.oldText: JAQUES. I prithee, pretty youth, let me be better acquainted with thee.

12.34.oldText: ROSALIND. They say you are a melancholy fellow.

12.35.oldText: JAQUES. I am so; I do love it better than laughing.

12.36.oldText: ROSALIND. Those that are in extremity of either are abominable fellows, and betray themselves to every modern censure worse than drunkards.

12.37.oldText: JAQUES. Why, 'tis good to be sad and say nothing.

12.38.oldText: ROSALIND. Why then, 'tis good to be a post.

12.39.oldText: JAQUES. I have neither the scholar's melancholy, which is emulation; nor the musician's, which is fantastical; nor the courtier's, which is proud; nor the soldier's, which is ambitious; nor the lawyer's, which is politic; nor the lady's, which is nice; nor the lover's, which is all these; but it is a melancholy of mine own, compounded of many simples, extracted from many objects, and, indeed, the sundry contemplation of my travels; in which my often rumination wraps me in a most humorous sadness.

12.40.oldText: ROSALIND. A traveller! By my faith, you have great reason to be sad. I fear you have sold your own lands to see other men's; then to have seen much and to have nothing is to have rich eyes and poor hands.

12.41.oldText: JAQUES. Yes, I have gain'd my experience.

12.43.oldText: ROSALIND. And your experience makes you sad. I had rather have a fool to make me merry than experience to make me sad- and to travel for it too.

12.44.oldText: ORLANDO. Good day, and happiness, dear Rosalind!

12.45.oldText: JAQUES. Nay, then, God buy you, an you talk in blank verse.

12.46.oldText: ROSALIND. Farewell, Monsieur Traveller; look you lisp and wear strange suits, disable all the benefits of your own country, be out of love with your nativity, and almost chide God for making you that countenance you are; or I will scarce think you have swam in a gondola. [Exit JAQUES] Why, how now, Orlando! where have you been all this while? You a lover! An you serve me such another trick, never come in my sight more.

12.47.oldText: ORLANDO. My fair Rosalind, I come within an hour of my promise.

12.48.oldText: ROSALIND. Break an hour's promise in love! He that will divide a minute into a thousand parts, and break but a part of the thousand part of a minute in the affairs of love, it may be said of him that Cupid hath clapp'd him o' th' shoulder, but I'll warrant him heart-whole.

12.50.oldText: ROSALIND. Nay, an you be so tardy, come no more in my sight. I had as lief be woo'd of a snail.

12.52.oldText: ROSALIND. Ay, of a snail; for though he comes slowly, he carries his house on his head- a better jointure, I think, than you make a woman; besides, he brings his destiny with him.

12.54.oldText: ROSALIND. Why, horns; which such as you are fain to be beholding to your wives for; but he comes armed in his fortune, and prevents the slander of his wife.

12.55.oldText: ORLANDO. Virtue is no horn-maker; and my Rosalind is virtuous.

12.56.oldText: ROSALIND. And I am your Rosalind.

12.57.oldText: CELIA. It pleases him to call you so; but he hath a Rosalind of a better leer than you.

12.58.oldText: ROSALIND. Come, woo me, woo me; for now I am in a holiday humour, and like enough to consent. What would you say to me now, an I were your very very Rosalind?

12.59.oldText: ORLANDO. I would kiss before I spoke.

12.60.oldText: ROSALIND. Nay, you were better speak first; and when you were gravell'd for lack of matter, you might take occasion to kiss. Very good orators, when they are out, they will spit; and for lovers lacking- God warn us!- matter, the cleanliest shift is to kiss.

12.61.oldText: ORLANDO. How if the kiss be denied?

12.62.oldText: ROSALIND. Then she puts you to entreaty, and there begins new matter.

12.63.oldText: ORLANDO. Who could be out, being before his beloved mistress?

12.64.oldText: ROSALIND. Marry, that should you, if I were your mistress; or I should think my honesty ranker than my wit.

12.66.oldText: ROSALIND. Not out of your apparel, and yet out of your suit. Am not I your Rosalind?

12.67.oldText: ORLANDO. I take some joy to say you are, because I would be talking of her.

12.68.oldText: ROSALIND. Well, in her person, I say I will not have you.

12.69.oldText: ORLANDO. Then, in mine own person, I die.

12.70.oldText: ROSALIND. No, faith, die by attorney. The poor world is almost six thousand years old, and in all this time there was not any man died in his own person, videlicet, in a love-cause. Troilus had his brains dash'd out with a Grecian club; yet he did what he could to die before, and he is one of the patterns of love. Leander, he would have liv'd many a fair year, though Hero had turn'd nun, if it had not been for a hot midsummer night; for, good youth, he went but forth to wash him in the Hellespont, and, being taken with the cramp, was drown'd; and the foolish chroniclers of that age found it was- Hero of Sestos. But these are all lies: men have died from time to time, and worms have eaten them, but not for love.

12.71.oldText: ORLANDO. I would not have my right Rosalind of this mind; for, I protest, her frown might kill me.

12.72.oldText: ROSALIND. By this hand, it will not kill a fly. But come, now I will be your Rosalind in a more coming-on disposition; and ask me what you will, I will grant it.

12.74.oldText: ROSALIND. Yes, faith, will I, Fridays and Saturdays, and all.

12.75.oldText: ORLANDO. And wilt thou have me?

12.80.oldText: ROSALIND. Why then, can one desire too much of a good thing? Come, sister, you shall be the priest, and marry us. Give me your hand, Orlando. What do you say, sister?

12.82.oldText: CELIA. I cannot say the words.

12.83.oldText: ROSALIND. You must begin 'Will you, Orlando'-

12.84.oldText: CELIA. Go to. Will you, Orlando, have to wife this Rosalind?

12.87.oldText: ORLANDO. Why, now; as fast as she can marry us.

12.88.oldText: ROSALIND. Then you must say 'I take thee, Rosalind, for wife.'

12.89.oldText: ORLANDO. I take thee, Rosalind, for wife.

12.90.oldText: ROSALIND. I might ask you for your commission; but- I do take thee, Orlando, for my husband. There's a girl goes before the priest; and, certainly, a woman's thought runs before her actions.

12.91.oldText: ORLANDO. So do all thoughts; they are wing'd.

12.92.oldText: ROSALIND. Now tell me how long you would have her, after you have possess'd her.

12.93.oldText: ORLANDO. For ever and a day.

12.94.oldText: ROSALIND. Say 'a day' without the 'ever.' No, no, Orlando; men are April when they woo, December when they wed: maids are May when they are maids, but the sky changes when they are wives. I will be more jealous of thee than a Barbary cock-pigeon over his hen, more clamorous than a parrot against rain, more new-fangled than an ape, more giddy in my desires than a monkey. I will weep for nothing, like Diana in the fountain, and I will do that when you are dispos'd to be merry; I will laugh like a hyen, and that when thou are inclin'd to sleep.

12.95.oldText: ORLANDO. But will my Rosalind do so?

12.96.oldText: ROSALIND. By my life, she will do as I do.

12.97.oldText: ORLANDO. O, but she is wise.

12.98.oldText: ROSALIND. Or else she could not have the wit to do this. The wiser, the waywarder. Make the doors upon a woman's wit, and it will out at the casement; shut that, and 'twill out at the key-hole; stop that, 'twill fly with the smoke out at the chimney.

12.99.oldText: ORLANDO. A man that had a wife with such a wit, he might say 'Wit, whither wilt?' ROSALIND. Nay, you might keep that check for it, till you met your wife's wit going to your neighbour's bed.

12.100.oldText: ORLANDO. And what wit could wit have to excuse that?

12.101.oldText: ROSALIND. Marry, to say she came to seek you there. You shall never take her without her answer, unless you take her without her tongue. O, that woman that cannot make her fault her husband's occasion, let her never nurse her child herself, for she will breed it like a fool!

12.102.oldText: ORLANDO. For these two hours, Rosalind, I will leave thee.

12.103.oldText: ROSALIND. Alas, dear love, I cannot lack thee two hours!

12.104.oldText: ORLANDO. I must attend the Duke at dinner; by two o'clock I will be with thee again.

12.105.oldText: ROSALIND. Ay, go your ways, go your ways. I knew what you would prove; my friends told me as much, and I thought no less. That flattering tongue of yours won me. 'Tis but one cast away, and so, come death! Two o'clock is your hour?

12.107.oldText: ROSALIND. By my troth, and in good earnest, and so God mend me, and by all pretty oaths that are not dangerous, if you break one jot of your promise, or come one minute behind your hour, I will think you the most pathetical break-promise, and the most hollow lover, and the most unworthy of her you call Rosalind, that may be chosen out of the gross band of the unfaithful. Therefore beware my censure, and keep your promise.

12.108.oldText: ORLANDO. With no less religion than if thou wert indeed my Rosalind; so, adieu.

12.109.oldText: ROSALIND. Well, Time is the old justice that examines all such offenders, and let Time try. Adieu. Exit ORLANDO

12.110.oldText: CELIA. You have simply misus'd our sex in your love-prate. We must have your doublet and hose pluck'd over your head, and show the world what the bird hath done to her own nest.

12.111.oldText: ROSALIND. O coz, coz, coz, my pretty little coz, that thou didst know how many fathom deep I am in love! But it cannot be sounded; my affection hath an unknown bottom, like the Bay of Portugal.

12.112.oldText: CELIA. Or rather, bottomless; that as fast as you pour affection in, it runs out.

12.113.oldText: ROSALIND. No; that same wicked bastard of Venus, that was begot of thought, conceiv'd of spleen, and born of madness; that blind rascally boy, that abuses every one's eyes, because his own are out- let him be judge how deep I am in love. I'll tell thee, Aliena, I cannot be out of the sight of Orlando. I'll go find a shadow, and sigh till he come.

13.1.oldText: Enter JAQUES and LORDS, in the habit of foresters

13.2.oldText: JAQUES. Which is he that killed the deer?

13.4.oldText: JAQUES. Let's present him to the Duke, like a Roman conqueror; and it would do well to set the deer's horns upon his head for a branch of victory. Have you no song, forester, for this purpose?

13.6.oldText: JAQUES. Sing it; 'tis no matter how it be in tune, so it make noise enough.

13.8.oldText: What shall he have that kill'd the deer? His leather skin and horns to wear.

13.11.oldText: Take thou no scorn to wear the horn; It was a crest ere thou wast born. Thy father's father wore it; And thy father bore it. The horn, the horn, the lusty horn, Is not a thing to laugh to scorn. Exeunt

14.2.oldText: ROSALIND. How say you now? Is it not past two o'clock? And here much Orlando!

14.3.oldText: CELIA. I warrant you, with pure love and troubled brain, he hath ta'en his bow and arrows, and is gone forth- to sleep. Look, who comes here.

14.5.oldText: SILVIUS. My errand is to you, fair youth; My gentle Phebe did bid me give you this. I know not the contents; but, as I guess By the stern brow and waspish action Which she did use as she was writing of it, It bears an angry tenour. Pardon me, I am but as a guiltless messenger.

14.6.oldText: ROSALIND. Patience herself would startle at this letter, And play the swaggerer. Bear this, bear all. She says I am not fair, that I lack manners; She calls me proud, and that she could not love me, Were man as rare as Phoenix. 'Od's my will! Her love is not the hare that I do hunt; Why writes she so to me? Well, shepherd, well, This is a letter of your own device.

14.7.oldText: SILVIUS. No, I protest, I know not the contents; Phebe did write it.

14.8.oldText: ROSALIND. Come, come, you are a fool, And turn'd into the extremity of love. I saw her hand; she has a leathern hand, A freestone-colour'd hand; I verily did think That her old gloves were on, but 'twas her hands; She has a huswife's hand- but that's no matter. I say she never did invent this letter: This is a man's invention, and his hand.

14.10.oldText: ROSALIND. Why, 'tis a boisterous and a cruel style; A style for challengers. Why, she defies me, Like Turk to Christian. Women's gentle brain Could not drop forth such giant-rude invention, Such Ethiope words, blacker in their effect Than in their countenance. Will you hear the letter?

14.11.oldText: SILVIUS. So please you, for I never heard it yet; Yet heard too much of Phebe's cruelty.

14.12.oldText: ROSALIND. She Phebes me: mark how the tyrant writes.

14.14.oldText: 'Art thou god to shepherd turn'd, That a maiden's heart hath burn'd?'

14.17.oldText: ROSALIND. 'Why, thy godhead laid apart, Warr'st thou with a woman's heart?'

14.18.oldText: Did you ever hear such railing?

14.19.oldText: 'Whiles the eye of man did woo me, That could do no vengeance to me.'

14.21.oldText: 'If the scorn of your bright eyne Have power to raise such love in mine, Alack, in me what strange effect Would they work in mild aspect! Whiles you chid me, I did love; How then might your prayers move! He that brings this love to the Little knows this love in me; And by him seal up thy mind, Whether that thy youth and kind Will the faithful offer take Of me and all that I can make; Or else by him my love deny, And then I'll study how to die.'

14.24.oldText: ROSALIND. Do you pity him? No, he deserves no pity. Wilt thou love such a woman? What, to make thee an instrument, and play false strains upon thee! Not to be endur'd! Well, go your way to her, for I see love hath made thee tame snake, and say this to her- that if she love me, I charge her to love thee; if she will not, I will never have her unless thou entreat for her. If you be a true lover, hence, and not a word; for here comes more company. Exit SILVIUS

14.26.oldText: OLIVER. Good morrow, fair ones; pray you, if you know, Where in the purlieus of this forest stands A sheep-cote fenc'd about with olive trees?

14.27.oldText: CELIA. West of this place, down in the neighbour bottom. The rank of osiers by the murmuring stream Left on your right hand brings you to the place. But at this hour the house doth keep itself; There's none within.

14.28.oldText: OLIVER. If that an eye may profit by a tongue, Then should I know you by description- Such garments, and such years: 'The boy is fair, Of female favour, and bestows himself Like a ripe sister; the woman low, And browner than her brother.' Are not you The owner of the house I did inquire for?

14.29.oldText: CELIA. It is no boast, being ask'd, to say we are.

14.30.oldText: OLIVER. Orlando doth commend him to you both; And to that youth he calls his Rosalind He sends this bloody napkin. Are you he?

14.31.oldText: ROSALIND. I am. What must we understand by this?

14.32.oldText: OLIVER. Some of my shame; if you will know of me What man I am, and how, and why, and where, This handkercher was stain'd.

14.33.oldText: CELIA. I pray you, tell it.

14.34.oldText: OLIVER. When last the young Orlando parted from you, He left a promise to return again Within an hour; and, pacing through the forest, Chewing the food of sweet and bitter fancy, Lo, what befell! He threw his eye aside, And mark what object did present itself. Under an oak, whose boughs were moss'd with age, And high top bald with dry antiquity, A wretched ragged man, o'ergrown with hair, Lay sleeping on his back. About his neck A green and gilded snake had wreath'd itself, Who with her head nimble in threats approach'd The opening of his mouth; but suddenly, Seeing Orlando, it unlink'd itself, And with indented glides did slip away Into a bush; under which bush's shade A lioness, with udders all drawn dry, Lay couching, head on ground, with catlike watch, When that the sleeping man should stir; for 'tis The royal disposition of that beast To prey on nothing that doth seem as dead. This seen, Orlando did approach the man, And found it was his brother, his elder brother.

14.35.oldText: CELIA. O, I have heard him speak of that same brother; And he did render him the most unnatural That liv'd amongst men.

14.36.oldText: OLIVER. And well he might so do, For well I know he was unnatural.

14.37.oldText: ROSALIND. But, to Orlando: did he leave him there, Food to the suck'd and hungry lioness?

14.38.oldText: OLIVER. Twice did he turn his back, and purpos'd so; But kindness, nobler ever than revenge, And nature, stronger than his just occasion, Made him give battle to the lioness, Who quickly fell before him; in which hurtling From miserable slumber I awak'd.

14.41.oldText: CELIA. Was't you that did so oft contrive to kill him?

14.42.oldText: OLIVER. 'Twas I; but 'tis not I. I do not shame To tell you what I was, since my conversion So sweetly tastes, being the thing I am.

14.43.oldText: ROSALIND. But for the bloody napkin?

14.44.oldText: OLIVER. By and by. When from the first to last, betwixt us two, Tears our recountments had most kindly bath'd, As how I came into that desert place- In brief, he led me to the gentle Duke, Who gave me fresh array and entertainment, Committing me unto my brother's love; Who led me instantly unto his cave, There stripp'd himself, and here upon his arm The lioness had torn some flesh away, Which all this while had bled; and now he fainted, And cried, in fainting, upon Rosalind. Brief, I recover'd him, bound up his wound, And, after some small space, being strong at heart, He sent me hither, stranger as I am, To tell this story, that you might excuse His broken promise, and to give this napkin, Dy'd in his blood, unto the shepherd youth That he in sport doth call his Rosalind.

14.46.oldText: CELIA. Why, how now, Ganymede! sweet Ganymede!

14.47.oldText: OLIVER. Many will swoon when they do look on blood.

14.48.oldText: CELIA. There is more in it. Cousin Ganymede!

14.50.oldText: ROSALIND. I would I were at home.

14.51.oldText: CELIA. We'll lead you thither. I pray you, will you take him by the arm?

14.52.oldText: OLIVER. Be of good cheer, youth. You a man! You lack a man's heart.

14.53.oldText: ROSALIND. I do so, I confess it. Ah, sirrah, a body would think this was well counterfeited. I pray you tell your brother how well I counterfeited. Heigh-ho!

14.54.oldText: OLIVER. This was not counterfeit; there is too great testimony in your complexion that it was a passion of earnest.

14.56.oldText: OLIVER. Well then, take a good heart and counterfeit to be a man.

14.57.oldText: ROSALIND. So I do; but, i' faith, I should have been a woman by right.

14.58.oldText: CELIA. Come, you look paler and paler; pray you draw homewards. Good sir, go with us.

14.59.oldText: OLIVER. That will I, for I must bear answer back How you excuse my brother, Rosalind.

14.60.oldText: ROSALIND. I shall devise something; but, I pray you, commend my counterfeiting to him. Will you go? Exeunt

14.67.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. We shall find a time, Audrey; patience, gentle Audrey.

14.68.oldText: AUDREY. Faith, the priest was good enough, for all the old gentleman's saying.

14.69.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. A most wicked Sir Oliver, Audrey, a most vile Martext. But, Audrey, there is a youth here in the forest lays claim to you.

14.70.oldText: AUDREY. Ay, I know who 'tis; he hath no interest in me in the world; here comes the man you mean.

14.72.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. It is meat and drink to me to see a clown. By my troth, we that have good wits have much to answer for: we shall be flouting; we cannot hold.

14.74.oldText: AUDREY. God ye good ev'n, William.

14.75.oldText: WILLIAM. And good ev'n to you, sir.

14.76.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. Good ev'n, gentle friend. Cover thy head, cover thy head; nay, prithee be cover'd. How old are you, friend?

14.78.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. A ripe age. Is thy name William?

14.80.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. A fair name. Wast born i' th' forest here?

14.81.oldText: WILLIAM. Ay, sir, I thank God.

14.82.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. 'Thank God.' A good answer. Art rich?

14.84.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. 'So so' is good, very good, very excellent good; and yet it is not; it is but so so. Art thou wise?

14.85.oldText: WILLIAM. Ay, sir, I have a pretty wit.

14.86.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. Why, thou say'st well. I do now remember a saying: 'The fool doth think he is wise, but the wise man knows himself to be a fool.' The heathen philosopher, when he had a desire to eat a grape, would open his lips when he put it into his mouth; meaning thereby that grapes were made to eat and lips to open. You do love this maid?

14.88.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. Give me your hand. Art thou learned?

14.90.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. Then learn this of me: to have is to have; for it is a figure in rhetoric that drink, being pour'd out of cup into a glass, by filling the one doth empty the other; for all your writers do consent that ipse is he; now, you are not ipse, for I am he.

14.92.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. He, sir, that must marry this woman. Therefore, you clown, abandon- which is in the vulgar leave- the society- which in the boorish is company- of this female- which in the common is woman- which together is: abandon the society of this female; or, clown, thou perishest; or, to thy better understanding, diest; or, to wit, I kill thee, make thee away, translate thy life into death, thy liberty into bondage. I will deal in poison with thee, or in bastinado, or in steel; I will bandy with thee in faction; will o'er-run thee with policy; I will kill thee a hundred and fifty ways; therefore tremble and depart.

14.94.oldText: WILLIAM. God rest you merry, sir. Exit

14.96.oldText: CORIN. Our master and mistress seeks you; come away, away.

14.97.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. Trip, Audrey, trip, Audrey. I attend, I attend. Exeunt

15.2.oldText: ORLANDO. Is't possible that on so little acquaintance you should like her? that but seeing you should love her? and loving woo? and, wooing, she should grant? and will you persever to enjoy her?

15.3.oldText: OLIVER. Neither call the giddiness of it in question, the poverty of her, the small acquaintance, my sudden wooing, nor her sudden consenting; but say with me, I love Aliena; say with her that she loves me; consent with both that we may enjoy each other. It shall be to your good; for my father's house and all the revenue that was old Sir Rowland's will I estate upon you, and here live and die a shepherd.

15.4.oldText: ORLANDO. You have my consent. Let your wedding be to-morrow. Thither will I invite the Duke and all's contented followers. Go you and prepare Aliena; for, look you, here comes my Rosalind.

15.7.oldText: OLIVER. And you, fair sister. Exit

15.8.oldText: ROSALIND. O, my dear Orlando, how it grieves me to see thee wear thy heart in a scarf!

15.10.oldText: ROSALIND. I thought thy heart had been wounded with the claws of a lion.

15.11.oldText: ORLANDO. Wounded it is, but with the eyes of a lady.

15.12.oldText: ROSALIND. Did your brother tell you how I counterfeited to swoon when he show'd me your handkercher?

15.13.oldText: ORLANDO. Ay, and greater wonders than that.

15.14.oldText: ROSALIND. O, I know where you are. Nay, 'tis true. There was never any thing so sudden but the fight of two rams and Caesar's thrasonical brag of 'I came, saw, and overcame.' For your brother and my sister no sooner met but they look'd; no sooner look'd but they lov'd; no sooner lov'd but they sigh'd; no sooner sigh'd but they ask'd one another the reason; no sooner knew the reason but they sought the remedy- and in these degrees have they made pair of stairs to marriage, which they will climb incontinent, or else be incontinent before marriage. They are in the very wrath of

15.15.oldText: love, and they will together. Clubs cannot part them.

15.16.oldText: ORLANDO. They shall be married to-morrow; and I will bid the Duke to the nuptial. But, O, how bitter a thing it is to look into happiness through another man's eyes! By so much the more shall I to-morrow be at the height of heart-heaviness, by how much I shall think my brother happy in having what he wishes for.

15.17.oldText: ROSALIND. Why, then, to-morrow I cannot serve your turn for Rosalind?

15.18.oldText: ORLANDO. I can live no longer by thinking.

15.19.oldText: ROSALIND. I will weary you, then, no longer with idle talking. Know of me then- for now I speak to some purpose- that I know you are a gentleman of good conceit. I speak not this that you should bear a good opinion of my knowledge, insomuch I say I know you are; neither do I labour for a greater esteem than may in some little measure draw a belief from you, to do yourself good, and not to grace me. Believe then, if you please, that I can do strange things. I have, since I was three year old, convers'd with a magician, most profound in his art and yet not damnable. If you do love Rosalind so near the heart as your gesture cries it out, when your brother marries Aliena shall you marry her. I know into what straits of fortune she is driven; and it is not impossible to me, if it appear not inconvenient to you, to set her before your eyes to-morrow, human as she is, and without any danger.

15.20.oldText: ORLANDO. Speak'st thou in sober meanings?

15.21.oldText: ROSALIND. By my life, I do; which I tender dearly, though I say I am a magician. Therefore put you in your best array, bid your friends; for if you will be married to-morrow, you shall; and to Rosalind, if you will.

15.23.oldText: Look, here comes a lover of mine, and a lover of hers.

15.24.oldText: PHEBE. Youth, you have done me much ungentleness To show the letter that I writ to you.

15.25.oldText: ROSALIND. I care not if I have. It is my study To seem despiteful and ungentle to you. You are there follow'd by a faithful shepherd; Look upon him, love him; he worships you.

15.26.oldText: PHEBE. Good shepherd, tell this youth what 'tis to love.

15.27.oldText: SILVIUS. It is to be all made of sighs and tears; And so am I for Phebe.

15.30.oldText: ROSALIND. And I for no woman.

15.31.oldText: SILVIUS. It is to be all made of faith and service; And so am I for Phebe.

15.34.oldText: ROSALIND. And I for no woman.

15.35.oldText: SILVIUS. It is to be all made of fantasy, All made of passion, and all made of wishes; All adoration, duty, and observance, All humbleness, all patience, and impatience, All purity, all trial, all obedience; And so am I for Phebe.

15.36.oldText: PHEBE. And so am I for Ganymede.

15.37.oldText: ORLANDO. And so am I for Rosalind.

15.38.oldText: ROSALIND. And so am I for no woman.

15.39.oldText: PHEBE. If this be so, why blame you me to love you?

15.40.oldText: SILVIUS. If this be so, why blame you me to love you?

15.41.oldText: ORLANDO. If this be so, why blame you me to love you?

15.42.oldText: ROSALIND. Why do you speak too, 'Why blame you me to love you?'

15.43.oldText: ORLANDO. To her that is not here, nor doth not hear.

15.44.oldText: ROSALIND. Pray you, no more of this; 'tis like the howling of Irish wolves against the moon. [To SILVIUS] I will help you if I can.

15.45.oldText: [To PHEBE] I would love you if I could.- To-morrow meet me

15.46.oldText: all together. [ To PHEBE ] I will marry you if ever I marry woman, and I'll be married to-morrow. [To ORLANDO] I will satisfy you if ever I satisfied man, and you shall be married to-morrow. [To Silvius] I will content you if what pleases you contents you, and you shall be married to-morrow. [To ORLANDO] As you love Rosalind, meet. [To SILVIUS] As you love Phebe, meet;- and as I love no woman, I'll meet. So, fare you well; I have left you commands.

15.47.oldText: SILVIUS. I'll not fail, if I live.

16.2.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. To-morrow is the joyful day, Audrey; to-morrow will we be married.

16.3.oldText: AUDREY. I do desire it with all my heart; and I hope it is no dishonest desire to desire to be a woman of the world. Here come two of the banish'd Duke's pages.

16.5.oldText: FIRST PAGE. Well met, honest gentleman.

16.6.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. By my troth, well met. Come sit, sit, and a song.

16.7.oldText: SECOND PAGE. We are for you; sit i' th' middle.

16.8.oldText: FIRST PAGE. Shall we clap into't roundly, without hawking, or spitting, or saying we are hoarse, which are the only prologues to a bad voice?

16.9.oldText: SECOND PAGE. I'faith, i'faith; and both in a tune, like two gipsies on a horse.

16.10.oldText: SONG. It was a lover and his lass, With a hey, and a ho, and a hey nonino, That o'er the green corn-field did pass In the spring time, the only pretty ring time, When birds do sing, hey ding a ding, ding. Sweet lovers love the spring.

16.11.oldText: Between the acres of the rye, With a hey, and a ho, and a hey nonino, These pretty country folks would lie, In the spring time, &c.

16.12.oldText: This carol they began that hour, With a hey, and a ho, and a hey nonino, How that a life was but a flower, In the spring time, &c.

16.13.oldText: And therefore take the present time, With a hey, and a ho, and a hey nonino, For love is crowned with the prime, In the spring time, &c.

16.14.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. Truly, young gentlemen, though there was no great matter in the ditty, yet the note was very untuneable.

16.15.oldText: FIRST PAGE. You are deceiv'd, sir; we kept time, we lost not our time.

16.16.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. By my troth, yes; I count it but time lost to hear such a foolish song. God buy you; and God mend your voices. Come, Audrey. Exeunt

17.1.oldText: Enter DUKE SENIOR, AMIENS, JAQUES, ORLANDO, OLIVER, and CELIA

17.2.oldText: DUKE SENIOR. Dost thou believe, Orlando, that the boy Can do all this that he hath promised?

17.3.oldText: ORLANDO. I sometimes do believe and sometimes do not: As those that fear they hope, and know they fear.

17.5.oldText: ROSALIND. Patience once more, whiles our compact is urg'd: You say, if I bring in your Rosalind, You will bestow her on Orlando here?

17.6.oldText: DUKE SENIOR. That would I, had I kingdoms to give with her.

17.7.oldText: ROSALIND. And you say you will have her when I bring her?

17.8.oldText: ORLANDO. That would I, were I of all kingdoms king.

17.9.oldText: ROSALIND. You say you'll marry me, if I be willing?

17.10.oldText: PHEBE. That will I, should I die the hour after.

17.11.oldText: ROSALIND. But if you do refuse to marry me, You'll give yourself to this most faithful shepherd?

17.13.oldText: ROSALIND. You say that you'll have Phebe, if she will?

17.14.oldText: SILVIUS. Though to have her and death were both one thing.

17.15.oldText: ROSALIND. I have promis'd to make all this matter even. Keep you your word, O Duke, to give your daughter; You yours, Orlando, to receive his daughter; Keep your word, Phebe, that you'll marry me, Or else, refusing me, to wed this shepherd; Keep your word, Silvius, that you'll marry her If she refuse me; and from hence I go, To make these doubts all even. Exeunt ROSALIND and CELIA

17.16.oldText: DUKE SENIOR. I do remember in this shepherd boy Some lively touches of my daughter's favour.

17.17.oldText: ORLANDO. My lord, the first time that I ever saw him Methought he was a brother to your daughter. But, my good lord, this boy is forest-born, And hath been tutor'd in the rudiments Of many desperate studies by his uncle, Whom he reports to be a great magician, Obscured in the circle of this forest.

17.19.oldText: JAQUES. There is, sure, another flood toward, and these couples are coming to the ark. Here comes a pair of very strange beasts which in all tongues are call'd fools.

17.20.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. Salutation and greeting to you all!

17.21.oldText: JAQUES. Good my lord, bid him welcome. This is the motley-minded gentleman that I have so often met in the forest. He hath been a courtier, he swears.

17.22.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. If any man doubt that, let him put me to my purgation. I have trod a measure; I have flatt'red a lady; I have been politic with my friend, smooth with mine enemy; I have undone three tailors; I have had four quarrels, and like to have fought one.

17.23.oldText: JAQUES. And how was that ta'en up?

17.24.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. Faith, we met, and found the quarrel was upon the seventh cause.

17.25.oldText: JAQUES. How seventh cause? Good my lord, like this fellow.

17.26.oldText: DUKE SENIOR. I like him very well.

17.27.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. God 'ild you, sir; I desire you of the like. I press in here, sir, amongst the rest of the country copulatives, to swear and to forswear, according as marriage binds and blood breaks. A poor virgin, sir, an ill-favour'd thing, sir, but mine own; a poor humour of mine, sir, to take that that man else will. Rich honesty dwells like a miser, sir, in a poor house; as your pearl in your foul oyster.

17.28.oldText: DUKE SENIOR. By my faith, he is very swift and sententious.

17.29.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. According to the fool's bolt, sir, and such dulcet diseases.

17.30.oldText: JAQUES. But, for the seventh cause: how did you find the quarrel on the seventh cause?

17.31.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. Upon a lie seven times removed- bear your body more seeming, Audrey- as thus, sir. I did dislike the cut of a certain courtier's beard; he sent me word, if I said his beard was not cut well, he was in the mind it was. This is call'd the Retort Courteous. If I sent him word again it was not well cut, he would send me word he cut it to please himself. This is call'd the Quip Modest. If again it was not well cut, he disabled my judgment. This is call'd the Reply Churlish. If again it was not well cut, he would answer I spake not true. This is call'd the Reproof Valiant. If again it was not well cut, he would say I lie. This is call'd the Countercheck Quarrelsome. And so to the Lie Circumstantial and the Lie Direct.

17.32.oldText: JAQUES. And how oft did you say his beard was not well cut?

17.33.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. I durst go no further than the Lie Circumstantial, nor he durst not give me the Lie Direct; and so we measur'd swords and parted.

17.34.oldText: JAQUES. Can you nominate in order now the degrees of the lie?

17.35.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. O, sir, we quarrel in print by the book, as you have books for good manners. I will name you the degrees. The first, the Retort Courteous; the second, the Quip Modest; the third, the Reply Churlish; the fourth, the Reproof Valiant; the fifth, the Countercheck Quarrelsome; the sixth, the Lie with Circumstance; the seventh, the Lie Direct. All these you may avoid but the Lie Direct; and you may avoid that too with an If. I knew when seven justices could not take up a quarrel; but when the parties were met themselves, one of them thought but of an If, as: 'If you

17.36.oldText: said so, then I said so.' And they shook hands, and swore brothers. Your If is the only peace-maker; much virtue in If.

17.37.oldText: JAQUES. Is not this a rare fellow, my lord? He's as good at any thing, and yet a fool.

17.38.oldText: DUKE SENIOR. He uses his folly like a stalking-horse, and under the presentation of that he shoots his wit.

17.39.oldText: Enter HYMEN, ROSALIND, and CELIA. Still MUSIC

17.40.oldText: HYMEN. Then is there mirth in heaven, When earthly things made even Atone together. Good Duke, receive thy daughter; Hymen from heaven brought her, Yea, brought her hither, That thou mightst join her hand with his, Whose heart within his bosom is.

17.41.oldText: ROSALIND. [To DUKE] To you I give myself, for I am yours.

17.42.oldText: [To ORLANDO] To you I give myself, for I am yours.

17.43.oldText: DUKE SENIOR. If there be truth in sight, you are my daughter.

17.44.oldText: ORLANDO. If there be truth in sight, you are my Rosalind.

17.45.oldText: PHEBE. If sight and shape be true, Why then, my love adieu!

17.46.oldText: ROSALIND. I'll have no father, if you be not he; I'll have no husband, if you be not he; Nor ne'er wed woman, if you be not she.

17.47.oldText: HYMEN. Peace, ho! I bar confusion; 'Tis I must make conclusion Of these most strange events. Here's eight that must take hands To join in Hymen's bands, If truth holds true contents. You and you no cross shall part; You and you are heart in heart; You to his love must accord, Or have a woman to your lord; You and you are sure together, As the winter to foul weather. Whiles a wedlock-hymn we sing, Feed yourselves with questioning, That reason wonder may diminish, How thus we met, and these things finish.

17.48.oldText: SONG Wedding is great Juno's crown; O blessed bond of board and bed! 'Tis Hymen peoples every town; High wedlock then be honoured. Honour, high honour, and renown, To Hymen, god of every town!

17.49.oldText: DUKE SENIOR. O my dear niece, welcome thou art to me! Even daughter, welcome in no less degree.

17.50.oldText: PHEBE. I will not eat my word, now thou art mine; Thy faith my fancy to thee doth combine.

17.52.oldText: JAQUES de BOYS. Let me have audience for a word or two. I am the second son of old Sir Rowland, That bring these tidings to this fair assembly. Duke Frederick, hearing how that every day Men of great worth resorted to this forest, Address'd a mighty power; which were on foot, In his own conduct, purposely to take His brother here, and put him to the sword; And to the skirts of this wild wood he came, Where, meeting with an old religious man, After some question with him, was converted Both from his enterprise and from the world; His crown bequeathing to his banish'd brother, And all their lands restor'd to them again That were with him exil'd. This to be true I do engage my life.

17.53.oldText: DUKE SENIOR. Welcome, young man. Thou offer'st fairly to thy brothers' wedding: To one, his lands withheld; and to the other, A land itself at large, a potent dukedom. First, in this forest let us do those ends That here were well begun and well begot; And after, every of this happy number, That have endur'd shrewd days and nights with us, Shall share the good of our returned fortune, According to the measure of their states. Meantime, forget this new-fall'n dignity, And fall into our rustic revelry. Play, music; and you brides and bridegrooms all, With measure heap'd in joy, to th' measures fall.

17.54.oldText: JAQUES. Sir, by your patience. If I heard you rightly, The Duke hath put on a religious life, And thrown into neglect the pompous court.

17.56.oldText: JAQUES. To him will I. Out of these convertites There is much matter to be heard and learn'd.

17.57.oldText: [To DUKE] You to your former honour I bequeath;

17.58.oldText: Your patience and your virtue well deserves it.

17.59.oldText: [To ORLANDO] You to a love that your true faith doth merit;

17.60.oldText: [To OLIVER] You to your land, and love, and great allies

17.61.oldText: [To SILVIUS] You to a long and well-deserved bed;

17.62.oldText: [To TOUCHSTONE] And you to wrangling; for thy loving voyage

17.63.oldText: Is but for two months victuall'd.- So to your pleasures; I am for other than for dancing measures.

17.65.oldText: JAQUES. To see no pastime I. What you would have I'll stay to know at your abandon'd cave. Exit

17.66.oldText: DUKE SENIOR. Proceed, proceed. We will begin these rites, As we do trust they'll end, in true delights. [A dance] Exeunt

17.69.oldText: ROSALIND. It is not the fashion to see the lady the epilogue; but it is no more unhandsome than to see the lord the prologue. If it be true that good wine needs no bush, 'tis true that a good play needs no epilogue. Yet to good wine they do use good bushes; and good plays prove the better by the help of good epilogues. What a case am I in then, that am neither a good epilogue, nor cannot insinuate with you in the behalf of a good play! I am not furnish'd like a beggar; therefore to beg will not become me. My way is to conjure you; and I'll begin with the women. I charge you, O women, for the love you bear to men, to like as much of this play as please you; and I charge you, O men, for the love you bear to women- as I perceive by your simp'ring none of you hates them- that between you and the women the play may please. If I were a woman, I would kiss as many of you as had beards that pleas'd me, complexions that lik'd me, and breaths that I defied not; and, I am sure, as many as have good beards, or good faces, or sweet breaths, will, for my kind offer, when I make curtsy, bid me farewell.

1.0.oldText: A lawn before the DUKE'S palace

1.2.oldText: CELIA. Please, Rosalind, sweet cousin, be cheerful.

1.3.oldText: ROSALIND. Dear Celia, I'm showing more cheer than I actually feel, and you'd have me even merrier than that? Unless you can teach me to forget a banished father, you can't teach me how to remember any extraordinary pleasure.

1.4.oldText: CELIA. I can see you don't love me with the full weight that I love you. If my uncle, your banished father, had banished your uncle—the Duke, my father—and you had stayed here with me, I could have taught my love to take your father as my own. You'd have done the same, if the truth of your love for me were as righteously balanced as mine is for you.

1.5.oldText: ROSALIND. All right, I'll forget my own circumstances and rejoice in yours.

1.6.oldText: CELIA. You know my father has no child but me, and isn't likely to have any other. Truly, when he dies you'll be his heir. What he took from your father by force, I'll restore to you in affection. On my honor, I will—and if I break that oath, may I turn into a monster. So, my sweet Rose, my dear Rose, be merry.

1.7.oldText: ROSALIND. From now on I will, cousin, and we'll invent some pastimes. Let's see—what do you think of falling in love?

1.8.oldText: CELIA. By all means, do—as a sport. But don't love any man in earnest, and don't go further even in sport than you can safely retreat from with an honorable blush.

1.9.oldText: ROSALIND. What shall our sport be, then?

1.10.oldText: CELIA. Let's sit and mock the good housewife Fortune off her wheel, so that from now on her gifts will be handed out equally.

1.11.oldText: ROSALIND. I wish we could. Her favors are terribly misplaced; that generous blind woman makes her worst mistakes in what she gives to women.

1.12.oldText: CELIA. True—the ones she makes beautiful, she rarely makes virtuous; and the ones she makes virtuous, she makes very ugly.

1.13.oldText: ROSALIND. No, now you're shifting from Fortune's office to Nature's. Fortune rules over worldly gifts, not over the features Nature gives.

1.15.oldText: CELIA. No? When Nature has made a beautiful creature, can't Fortune throw her into the fire? Though Nature has given us wit to mock Fortune, hasn't Fortune sent in this fool to cut off the argument?

1.16.oldText: ROSALIND. Indeed, Fortune is too tough for Nature here—when Fortune uses one of Nature's naturals to cut off Nature's wit.

1.17.oldText: CELIA. Perhaps this isn't Fortune's doing either, but Nature's—who, seeing that our natural wits are too dull to reason about such goddesses, has sent this natural to be our whetstone. The dullness of the fool is always the whetstone of wits. Well now, wit! Where are you wandering?

1.18.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. Mistress, you're to come at once to your father.

1.19.oldText: CELIA. Were you made the messenger?

1.20.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. No, on my honor; but I was told to come fetch you.

1.21.oldText: ROSALIND. Where did you learn that oath, fool?

1.22.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. From a certain knight who swore by his honor that the pancakes were good, and swore by his honor that the mustard was bad. Now I'll insist the pancakes were bad and the mustard was good—and yet the knight wasn't forsworn.

1.23.oldText: CELIA. How do you prove that, out of the great heap of your knowledge?

1.24.oldText: ROSALIND. Yes, indeed, now unmuzzle your wisdom.

1.25.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. Both of you, step forward—stroke your chins and swear by your beards that I am a rogue.

1.26.oldText: CELIA. By our beards, if we had any, you are.

1.27.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. By my roguery, if I had any, then I would be. But if you swear by something that isn't there, you aren't forsworn. Neither was this knight, swearing by his honor—because he never had any. Or if he had any, he had sworn it away long before he ever saw those pancakes or that mustard.

1.28.oldText: CELIA. Please, who is it that you mean?

1.29.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. One whom old Frederick, your father, loves.

1.30.oldText: CELIA. My father's love is enough to honor him. Enough—say no more about him. You'll be whipped for slander one of these days.

1.31.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. All the more pity that fools may not speak wisely about what wise men do foolishly.

1.32.oldText: CELIA. By my faith, you're right. Ever since the little wit that fools have was silenced, the little foolishness that wise men have makes a great show. Here comes Monsieur Le Beau.

1.34.oldText: ROSALIND. With his mouth full of news.

1.35.oldText: CELIA. Which he'll stuff into us the way pigeons feed their young.

1.36.oldText: ROSALIND. Then we'll be crammed with news.

1.37.oldText: CELIA. All the better—we'll be more marketable. Bon jour, Monsieur Le Beau. What's the news?

1.38.oldText: LE BEAU. Fair Princess, you've missed some excellent sport.

1.40.oldText: LE BEAU. What color, madam? How shall I answer that?

1.41.oldText: ROSALIND. However wit and fortune decide.

1.42.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. Or however the Destinies decree.

1.43.oldText: CELIA. Well said—that was laid on with a trowel.

1.44.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. No, if I don't keep up my rank—

1.45.oldText: ROSALIND. You lose your old smell.

1.46.oldText: LE BEAU. You amaze me, ladies. I meant to tell you of some good wrestling that you've missed.

1.47.oldText: ROSALIND. Still—tell us how the wrestling went.

1.48.oldText: LE BEAU. I'll tell you the beginning, and if your ladyships

1.49.oldText: please, you may see the end—for the best is still to come, and they're coming right here, where you are, to perform it.

1.50.oldText: CELIA. Well then, the beginning—which is dead and buried.

1.51.oldText: LE BEAU. There comes an old man and his three sons—

1.52.oldText: CELIA. I could match this beginning with an old tale.

1.53.oldText: LE BEAU. Three handsome young men, of excellent stature and bearing.

1.54.oldText: ROSALIND. With notices around their necks: 'Be it known unto all men by these presents'—

1.55.oldText: LE BEAU. The eldest of the three wrestled with Charles, the Duke's wrestler. In an instant Charles threw him and broke three of his ribs, so there's little hope of life in him. He did the same to the second, and the same to the third. There they lie. The poor old father is making such pitiful lament over them that all the bystanders are weeping in sympathy.

1.57.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. But what's the sport, monsieur, that the ladies have missed?

1.58.oldText: LE BEAU. Why, this that I'm telling you about.

1.59.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. So men can grow wiser every day. It's the first time I ever heard breaking of ribs called sport for ladies.

1.60.oldText: CELIA. Same for me, I swear.

1.61.oldText: ROSALIND. But is there anyone else who longs to hear this broken music in his ribs? Is there another fan of rib-breaking out there? Shall we watch this wrestling, cousin?

1.62.oldText: LE BEAU. You'll have to, if you stay here. This is the spot appointed for the match, and they're ready to begin.

1.63.oldText: CELIA. Look, here they come. Let's stay and watch.

1.64.oldText: Flourish. Enter DUKE FREDERICK, LORDS, ORLANDO, CHARLES, and ATTENDANTS

1.65.oldText: FREDERICK. Get on with it. Since the youth won't be talked out of it, let the danger be on his own stubborn head.

1.66.oldText: ROSALIND. Is that the man over there?

1.67.oldText: LE BEAU. The very one, madam.

1.68.oldText: CELIA. Alas, he's too young—yet he has a successful look.

1.69.oldText: FREDERICK. Well now, daughter and niece! Have you crept in here to watch the wrestling?

1.70.oldText: ROSALIND. Yes, my lord—with your permission.

1.71.oldText: FREDERICK. You won't take much delight in it, I can tell you.

1.72.oldText: The match is so uneven. Out of pity for the challenger's youth I'd gladly dissuade him, but he won't listen. Speak to him, ladies—see if you can move him.

1.73.oldText: CELIA. Call him over, good Monsieur Le Beau.

1.74.oldText: FREDERICK. Do so; I'll step aside.

1.76.oldText: LE BEAU. Monsieur the Challenger, the Princess calls for you.

1.77.oldText: ORLANDO. I attend on them with all respect and duty.

1.78.oldText: ROSALIND. Young man, have you challenged Charles the wrestler?

1.79.oldText: ORLANDO. No, fair Princess—he's the one issuing the general challenge. I come in, like the others, to test the strength of my youth against him.

1.80.oldText: CELIA. Young gentleman, your spirits are too bold for your years. You've seen brutal proof of this man's strength. If you could see yourself with your own eyes, or know yourself by your own judgment, the fear of the attempt would advise you to a more even match. We beg you, for your own sake, embrace your safety and give up this attempt.

1.81.oldText: ROSALIND. Please, young sir—your reputation won't suffer for it. We'll make it our request to the Duke that the wrestling not go forward.

1.82.oldText: ORLANDO. I beg you, don't punish me with your harsh thoughts—I confess I'm very guilty in denying anything to such fair and excellent ladies. But let your fair eyes and gentle wishes go with me into the trial. If I'm defeated, only one is shamed who was never favored. If I'm killed, only one is dead who is willing to die. I'll do my friends no wrong, since I have none to mourn me. I'll do the world no harm, since I have nothing in it. I only fill up a place in the world—a place that may be better filled when I have emptied it.

1.83.oldText: ROSALIND. The little strength I have, I wish were with you.

1.84.oldText: CELIA. And mine to add to hers.

1.85.oldText: ROSALIND. Fare you well. I pray heaven I'm wrong about you!

1.86.oldText: CELIA. May your heart's desires go with you!

1.87.oldText: CHARLES. Come on—where's this young gallant who's so eager to lie down on his mother earth?

1.88.oldText: ORLANDO. Ready, sir—but his will works on a more modest plan than that.

1.89.oldText: FREDERICK. You'll try only one fall.

1.90.oldText: CHARLES. No, I assure your Grace, you won't have to talk him into a second—not after the trouble you had urging him out of the first.

1.91.oldText: ORLANDO. You plan to mock me afterward; you shouldn't have mocked me beforehand. Come on then.

1.92.oldText: ROSALIND. Now, may Hercules be your strength, young man!

1.93.oldText: CELIA. I wish I were invisible, to catch that strong fellow by the leg. [They wrestle]

1.95.oldText: CELIA. If I had a thunderbolt in my eye, I could tell you who'd go down.

1.98.oldText: ORLANDO. Yes, I beg your Grace—I'm not even out of breath yet.

1.100.oldText: LE BEAU. He can't speak, my lord.

1.101.oldText: FREDERICK. Carry him away. What is your name, young man?

1.102.oldText: ORLANDO. Orlando, my lord—the youngest son of Sir Rowland de Boys.

1.103.oldText: FREDERICK. I wish you had been the son of some other man. The world thought your father honorable, But I always found him to be my enemy. You would have pleased me better with this deed Had you come from a different house. But fare you well; you're a gallant youth. I wish you had named me a different father. Exeunt DUKE, train, and LE BEAU

1.104.oldText: CELIA. If I were my father, cousin, would I do this?

1.105.oldText: ORLANDO. I'm prouder to be Sir Rowland's son, His youngest son—and would not exchange that title To be adopted heir to Frederick.

1.106.oldText: ROSALIND. My father loved Sir Rowland as his own soul, And all the world shared my father's opinion. Had I known beforehand this young man was his son, I would have added tears to my pleading Before he should have risked himself like this.

1.107.oldText: CELIA. Gentle cousin, Let us go thank him, and encourage him; My father's rough and envious temper Cuts me to the heart. Sir, you've well deserved; If you keep your promises in love As justly as you've exceeded all promise here, Your mistress will be happy.

1.108.oldText: ROSALIND. Gentleman, [Giving him a chain from her neck] Wear this for me—from one who's out of favor with fortune, Who would give more, but her hand lacks the means. Shall we go, cousin?

1.109.oldText: CELIA. Yes. Fare you well, fair gentleman.

1.110.oldText: ORLANDO. Can't I even say 'I thank you'? My better parts Are all thrown down; and what stands up here Is only a quintain, a mere lifeless block.

1.111.oldText: ROSALIND. He calls us back. My pride fell with my fortunes; I'll ask him what he wants. Did you call, sir? Sir, you've wrestled well, and overthrown More than your enemies.

1.113.oldText: ROSALIND. I'm with you. Fare you well. Exeunt ROSALIND and CELIA

1.114.oldText: ORLANDO. What passion hangs these weights on my tongue? I cannot speak to her, though she invited conversation. O poor Orlando, you are overthrown! Either Charles or something weaker has mastered you.

1.116.oldText: LE BEAU. Good sir, I counsel you in friendship To leave this place. Although you have deserved High commendation, true applause, and love, Yet such is now the Duke's mood That he misconstrues all that you have done. The Duke is moody; what he is, indeed, Is more for you to imagine than for me to say.

1.117.oldText: ORLANDO. I thank you, sir; and please tell me this: Which of the two was daughter of the Duke Who was here at the wrestling?

1.118.oldText: LE BEAU. Neither, if we judge by manners; But the smaller one is indeed his daughter; The other is daughter to the banished Duke, And kept here by her usurping uncle To be his daughter's companion; their loves Are dearer than the natural bond of sisters. But I can tell you that lately this Duke Has taken displeasure against his gentle niece, Grounded on no other reason Than that the people praise her for her virtues And pity her for her good father's sake; And on my life, his malice against the lady Will suddenly burst out. Sir, fare you well. Hereafter, in a better world than this, I shall desire more love and knowledge of you.

1.119.oldText: ORLANDO. I'm much obliged to you; fare you well. Exit LE BEAU So I must pass from the smoke into the fire; From a tyrant Duke to a tyrant brother. But heavenly Rosalind! Exit

2.2.oldText: CELIA. Why, cousin! Why, Rosalind! Cupid have mercy! Not a word?

2.3.oldText: ROSALIND. Not one to throw at a dog.

2.4.oldText: CELIA. No, your words are too precious to waste on mongrels. Throw some of them at me. Come on, lame me with reasons.

2.5.oldText: ROSALIND. Then there'd be two cousins laid up—one lamed with reasons and the other mad without any.

2.6.oldText: CELIA. But is this all because of your father?

2.7.oldText: ROSALIND. No, some of it is because of my child's father. Oh, how full of briars is this working-day world!

2.8.oldText: CELIA. They're only burs, cousin, thrown on you in holiday foolery. If we don't walk in the well-worn paths, our very petticoats will catch them.

2.9.oldText: ROSALIND. I could shake those off my coat. But these burs are in my heart.

2.11.oldText: ROSALIND. I would try, if a cough of 'hem' could bring him to me.

2.12.oldText: CELIA. Come on, wrestle with your feelings.

2.13.oldText: ROSALIND. Oh, they're on the side of a better wrestler than I am.

2.14.oldText: CELIA. Well, good luck to you! You'll keep trying in time, despite the fall. But putting these jokes aside, let's talk seriously. Is it possible that all of a sudden you've fallen so hard for old Sir Rowland's youngest son?

2.15.oldText: ROSALIND. The Duke my father loved his father dearly.

2.16.oldText: CELIA. Does it follow then that you should love his son dearly? By that kind of logic I should hate him, because my father hated his father dearly. Yet I don't hate Orlando.

2.17.oldText: ROSALIND. No, by my faith—don't hate him, for my sake.

2.18.oldText: CELIA. Why shouldn't I? Doesn't he deserve to be hated?

2.20.oldText: ROSALIND. Let me love him for that, and you love him because I do. Look, here comes the Duke.

2.21.oldText: CELIA. With his eyes full of anger.

2.22.oldText: FREDERICK. Mistress, get out as fast as safety allows, And remove yourself from our court.

2.24.oldText: FREDERICK. You, niece. Within the next ten days, if you are found Within twenty miles of our public court, You die for it.

2.25.oldText: ROSALIND. I beg your Grace, Let me at least carry away knowledge of my offense. If I'm in touch with my own self, Or have any acquaintance with my own desires, If I'm not dreaming or out of my mind— And I trust I'm not—then, dear uncle, Not even by an unborn thought Have I offended your Highness.

2.26.oldText: FREDERICK. So all traitors talk. If their defense could be made in words, They'd be as innocent as grace itself. Let this be enough for you: I don't trust you.

2.27.oldText: ROSALIND. Yet your mistrust can't make me a traitor. Tell me, what is this suspicion based on?

2.28.oldText: FREDERICK. You are your father's daughter. That is enough.

2.29.oldText: ROSALIND. So I was when your Highness took his dukedom. So I was when your Highness banished him. Treason isn't inherited, my lord; And even if we did get it from our parents, What's that to me? My father was no traitor. So, my good lord, don't mistake me so much As to think my poverty is treacherous.

2.30.oldText: CELIA. Dear sovereign, hear me speak.

2.31.oldText: FREDERICK. Yes, Celia—we kept her here for your sake, Or else she would have gone wandering with her father.

2.32.oldText: CELIA. I didn't beg back then to have her stay; It was your pleasure and your own remorse. I was too young at the time to value her, But now I know her. If she's a traitor, Then so am I: we've always slept together, Risen at the same instant, learned, played, eaten together. And wherever we went, like Juno's swans, We went paired and inseparable.

2.33.oldText: FREDERICK. She is too clever for you; and her smoothness, Her very silence and her patience, Speak to the people, and they pity her. You are a fool. She robs you of your good name; And you'll shine brighter and seem more virtuous When she is gone. So don't open your lips. Firm and irrevocable is the doom I have passed on her: she is banished.

2.34.oldText: CELIA. Then pronounce that sentence on me too, my lord; I cannot live out of her company.

2.35.oldText: FREDERICK. You are a fool. You, niece—get yourself ready. If you overstay the time, on my honor, And on the weight of my word, you die. Exeunt DUKE and LORDS

2.36.oldText: CELIA. Oh my poor Rosalind! Where will you go? Will you change fathers? I'll give you mine. I beg you, don't be more grieved than I am.

2.37.oldText: ROSALIND. I have more reason to be.

2.38.oldText: CELIA. You do not, cousin. Please be cheerful. Don't you know the Duke Has banished me, his daughter?

2.40.oldText: CELIA. No, hasn't he? Then Rosalind lacks the love That teaches you that you and I are one. Shall we be sundered? Shall we part, sweet girl? No—let my father find another heir. So plan with me how we may flee, Where to go, and what to take with us; And don't try to take this burden on yourself, Bearing your griefs alone, and leaving me out; For, by this heaven now pale with our sorrows, Whatever you say, I'm going with you.

2.41.oldText: ROSALIND. Why, where shall we go?

2.42.oldText: CELIA. To seek my uncle in the Forest of Arden.

2.43.oldText: ROSALIND. Alas, what danger it will be for us, Maidens as we are, to travel so far! Beauty draws thieves sooner than gold.

2.44.oldText: CELIA. I'll put myself in poor and shabby clothes, And smudge my face with a kind of brown dye; You do the same. So we'll pass along And never attract attackers.

2.45.oldText: ROSALIND. Wouldn't it be better, Since I'm taller than the usual woman, That I dress in every detail like a man? A handsome cutlass at my thigh, A boar-spear in my hand—and in my heart, Whatever hidden woman's fear may lie— We'll wear a swaggering, martial outside, As many other mannish cowards do Who carry it off with appearances.

2.46.oldText: CELIA. What shall I call you when you're a man?

2.47.oldText: ROSALIND. I'll have no worse a name than Jove's own page, And therefore see that you call me Ganymede. But what will you be called?

2.48.oldText: CELIA. Something with a reference to my situation: No longer Celia, but Aliena.

2.49.oldText: ROSALIND. But, cousin, what if we tried to steal The clownish fool out of your father's court? Wouldn't he be a comfort on our travels?

2.50.oldText: CELIA. He'll come along over the wide world with me; Leave it to me to coax him. Let's go, And gather our jewels and our wealth together; Plan the fittest time and safest way To hide ourselves from the pursuit that will be made After my flight. Now we go in contentment To liberty, and not to banishment. Exeunt

2.56.oldText: Enter DUKE SENIOR, AMIENS, and two or three LORDS, like foresters

2.57.oldText: DUKE SENIOR. Now, my comrades and brothers in exile, Hasn't long custom made this life sweeter Than that of painted pomp? Aren't these woods More free from peril than the envious court? Here we don't feel Adam's punishment, The difference of the seasons—when the icy fang And churlish chiding of the winter wind Bite and blow upon my body, Even till I shrink with cold, I smile and say 'This is no flattery; these are counsellors That feelingly persuade me of what I am.' Sweet are the uses of adversity, Which, like the toad—ugly and venomous— Still wears a precious jewel in its head; And this life of ours, free from public haunt, Finds tongues in trees, books in running brooks, Sermons in stones, and good in everything. I would not change it.

2.58.oldText: AMIENS. Happy is your Grace, That can translate the stubbornness of fortune Into so quiet and so sweet a style.

2.59.oldText: DUKE SENIOR. Come, shall we go and kill some venison? And yet it pains me that the poor dappled creatures, Being native townsfolk of this wilderness city, Should, within their own bounds, with forked arrowheads Have their round haunches gored.

2.60.oldText: FIRST LORD. Indeed, my lord, The melancholy Jaques grieves at that; And on that score swears you usurp more Than your brother who has banished you. Today my Lord of Amiens and I Stole behind him as he lay stretched out Under an oak whose ancient root peeps out Over the brook that brawls along this wood! To that place a poor solitary stag, That from the hunter's aim had taken a wound, Came to languish; and indeed, my lord, The wretched animal heaved out such groans That their force stretched his leathery hide Almost to bursting; and the big round tears Coursed one after another down his innocent nose In piteous chase. And thus the hairy fool, Much watched by the melancholy Jaques, Stood on the extreme edge of the swift brook, Adding to it with his tears.

2.61.oldText: DUKE SENIOR. But what did Jaques say? Didn't he moralize this spectacle?

2.62.oldText: FIRST LORD. Oh yes, into a thousand similes. First, about the deer's weeping into the needless stream: 'Poor deer,' he said, 'you make a will Just as worldly people do, giving the bulk of your wealth To that which already has too much.' Then, being there alone, Left and abandoned by his velvet friends: ''Tis right,' said he, 'so misery parts The flow of company.' Soon afterward, a careless herd, Full from the pasture, jumps along past him And never stops to greet him. 'Yes,' said Jaques, 'Sweep on, you fat and greasy citizens; That's just the fashion. Why do you look At that poor and broken bankrupt there?' Thus most invectively he pierces through The body of the country, city, court, Yes, and of this life of ours; swearing that we Are mere usurpers, tyrants, and worse, To frighten the animals and kill them off In their assigned and native dwelling-place.

2.63.oldText: DUKE SENIOR. And did you leave him in this contemplation?

2.64.oldText: SECOND LORD. We did, my lord—weeping and commenting Upon the sobbing deer.

2.65.oldText: DUKE SENIOR. Show me the place. I love to engage him in these sullen moods, For then he's full of matter.

2.66.oldText: FIRST LORD. I'll bring you to him straight away. Exeunt

3.2.oldText: FREDERICK. Can it possibly be that no one saw them? It can't be; some villains of my court Are in on this, by consent or by negligence.

3.3.oldText: FIRST LORD. I can't find anyone who saw her. The ladies who attend her in her chamber Saw her in bed, and early in the morning They found the bed empty of their mistress.

3.4.oldText: SECOND LORD. My lord, the scurvy clown, at whom your Grace So often used to laugh, is also missing. Hisperia, the Princess's gentlewoman, Confesses that she secretly overheard Your daughter and her cousin praising at length The qualities and graces of the wrestler Who only lately threw the sinewy Charles; And she believes, wherever they have gone, That youth is surely in their company.

3.5.oldText: FREDERICK. Send to his brother. Fetch that gallant here. If he is absent, bring his brother to me; I'll make him find him. Do this at once; And don't let the search and inquiry slacken Until you bring back these foolish runaways. Exeunt

4.3.oldText: ADAM. What, my young master? Oh, my gentle master! Oh, my sweet master! Oh, you remembrance Of old Sir Rowland! Why, what are you doing here? Why are you virtuous? Why do people love you? And why are you gentle, strong, and valiant? Why would you be so foolish as to overcome The handsome champion of the moody Duke? Your praise has reached home too swiftly before you. Don't you know, master, that for some kinds of men Their graces serve them only as enemies? So it is with yours. Your virtues, gentle master, Are sanctified and holy traitors to you. Oh, what a world it is, when what is fine Poisons the one who carries it!

4.5.oldText: ADAM. Oh, unhappy young man! Don't come inside these doors; under this roof The enemy of all your graces lives. Your brother—no, no brother; yet the son— Yet not the son; I will not call him son Of the man I was about to call his father— Has heard your praises; and tonight he means To burn the lodging where you usually sleep, With you inside it. If he fails at that, He has other ways to cut you off. I overheard him and his schemes. This is no place for you; this house is just a slaughterhouse. Abhor it, fear it, do not enter it.

4.6.oldText: ORLANDO. Why, where, Adam, would you have me go?

4.7.oldText: ADAM. No matter where, so long as you don't come here.

4.8.oldText: ORLANDO. What, would you have me go and beg for my food, Or with a base and rough sword force A thievish living on the public road? That I must do, or I know not what to do; Yet that I will not do, however I can manage. I'd rather subject myself to the malice Of a degenerate and bloody brother.

4.9.oldText: ADAM. But don't do that. I have five hundred crowns, The thrifty wages I saved while under your father, Which I stored away to be my caregiver When my old limbs would no longer serve, And unregarded age was thrown into corners. Take it, and may He who feeds the ravens, Yes, providently caters for the sparrow, Be a comfort to my old age! Here is the gold; All of it I give to you. Let me be your servant. Though I look old, yet I am strong and lusty; For in my youth I never applied Hot and rebellious liquors to my blood, Nor with a shameless brow courted The means of weakness and debility. So my old age is like a hearty winter, Frosty, but kindly. Let me go with you; I'll do the work of a younger man In all your business and necessities.

4.10.oldText: ORLANDO. Oh, good old man, how well in you appears The steady service of the older world, When service sweated for duty, not for reward! You don't fit the fashion of these times, Where no one will sweat except for promotion, And once they have it, they choke off their service In the very having of it. It is not so with you. But, poor old man, you're pruning a rotten tree That can't produce so much as a blossom To repay all your pains and husbandry. But come along; we'll go together, And before we've spent your young man's wages We'll find some settled, modest contentment.

4.11.oldText: ADAM. Master, lead on; and I will follow you To the last gasp, with truth and loyalty. From seventeen years till now almost four-score I lived here, but now I live here no longer. At seventeen many seek their fortunes, But at fourscore it's too late in the week. Yet fortune can't reward me better Than to die well and not in my master's debt. Exeunt

5.1.oldText: Enter ROSALIND as GANYMEDE, CELIA as ALIENA, and CLOWN alias TOUCHSTONE

5.2.oldText: ROSALIND. Oh Jupiter, how weary my spirits are!

5.3.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. I wouldn't care about my spirits, if only my legs weren't weary.

5.4.oldText: ROSALIND. I could find it in my heart to disgrace my man's clothing and cry like a woman; but I must comfort the weaker vessel, since doublet and hose ought to show themselves courageous to petticoat. So, courage, good Aliena.

5.5.oldText: CELIA. Please, bear with me; I can't go any further.

5.6.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. For my part, I'd rather bear with you than carry you. Yet I'd be carrying no cross even if I did carry you, because I think you have no money in your purse.

5.7.oldText: ROSALIND. Well, this is the Forest of Arden.

5.8.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. Yes, now I'm in Arden—the bigger fool I. When I was at home, I was in a better place. But travelers must make do.

5.10.oldText: ROSALIND. Yes, do that, good Touchstone. Look, who's coming—a young man and an old one in earnest talk.

5.11.oldText: CORIN. That's the way to make her go on scorning you.

5.12.oldText: SILVIUS. Oh Corin, if you only knew how I love her!

5.13.oldText: CORIN. I can partly guess; I've loved in my time too.

5.14.oldText: SILVIUS. No, Corin, being old, you can't guess, Though in your youth you were as true a lover As ever sighed upon a midnight pillow. But if your love was ever like mine— And I'm sure no man ever loved so— How many utterly ridiculous things Were you drawn into by your fancy?

5.15.oldText: CORIN. Into a thousand that I've forgotten.

5.16.oldText: SILVIUS. Oh, then you never loved so wholeheartedly! If you don't remember the slightest folly That love ever made you run into, You haven't loved. Or if you haven't sat as I do now, Wearing out your listener with your mistress's praises, You haven't loved. Or if you haven't broken from company Abruptly, the way my passion makes me now, You haven't loved. Oh Phebe, Phebe, Phebe! Exit Silvius

5.17.oldText: ROSALIND. Alas, poor shepherd! By searching out your wound, I've stumbled by accident on my own.

5.18.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. And I on mine. I remember when I was in love, I broke my sword on a stone and told it to take that for coming at night to Jane Smile. And I remember kissing her laundry-bat, and the cow's udders that her pretty chapped hands had milked. And I remember wooing a peapod instead of her—from which I took two pods, and giving them to her, said with tears, 'Wear these for my sake.' We who are true lovers run into strange capers; but as all is mortal in nature, so all of nature in love is mortal in folly.

5.19.oldText: ROSALIND. You speak more wisely than you realize.

5.20.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. No, I'll never be aware of my own wit until I break my shins against it.

5.21.oldText: ROSALIND. Jove, Jove! This shepherd's passion Looks very much like my own.

5.22.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. And mine—though it's growing somewhat stale with me.

5.23.oldText: CELIA. Please, one of you ask that man over there Whether he'll give us any food for gold; I'm fainting almost to death.

5.25.oldText: ROSALIND. Quiet, fool; he's not your kinsman.

5.28.oldText: CORIN. Otherwise they're very wretched indeed.

5.29.oldText: ROSALIND. Quiet, I say. Good evening to you, friend.

5.30.oldText: CORIN. And to you, gentle sir, and to you all.

5.31.oldText: ROSALIND. Please, shepherd, if love or gold Can buy a meal in this wild place, Bring us where we may rest and eat. Here's a young maid much oppressed by travel, And fainting for relief.

5.32.oldText: CORIN. Fair sir, I pity her, And wish, for her sake more than my own, My fortunes were more able to relieve her. But I'm shepherd to another man, And I don't shear the fleeces that I graze. My master is of churlish disposition, And cares little to find the way to heaven By doing deeds of hospitality. Besides, his cottage, his flocks, and his pastures Are now up for sale; and at our sheepcote now, Because of his absence, there's nothing You'd want to eat. But what there is, come see, And by my voice you'll be most welcome.

5.33.oldText: ROSALIND. Who is it that will buy his flock and pasture?

5.34.oldText: CORIN. That young swain you saw here just a moment ago, Who cares little for buying anything.

5.35.oldText: ROSALIND. Please, if it's honest to do so, You buy the cottage, pasture, and the flock, And we'll give you the money to pay for it.

5.36.oldText: CELIA. And we'll improve your wages. I like this place, And willingly could spend my time in it.

5.37.oldText: CORIN. Certainly the thing is up for sale. Come with me. If you like, after looking it over— The soil, the profit, and this kind of life— I'll be your very faithful steward, And buy it with your gold right away. Exeunt

6.3.oldText: AMIENS. Under the greenwood tree Whoever loves to lie with me, And tune his merry note To the sweet bird's throat, Come hither, come hither, come hither. Here he shall see No enemy But winter and rough weather.

6.5.oldText: AMIENS. It will make you melancholy, Monsieur Jaques.

6.6.oldText: JAQUES. I'm grateful for that. More, please, more. I can suck melancholy out of a song the way a weasel sucks eggs. More, please, more.

6.7.oldText: AMIENS. My voice is rough; I know I can't please you.

6.8.oldText: JAQUES. I don't want you to please me; I want you to sing. Come on, more—another stanza. Do you call them stanzas?

6.9.oldText: AMIENS. Whatever you wish, Monsieur Jaques.

6.10.oldText: JAQUES. No, I don't care what they're called; they owe me nothing. Will you sing?

6.11.oldText: AMIENS. More to oblige you than to please myself.

6.12.oldText: JAQUES. Well then, if I ever thank any man, I'll thank you. But what they call compliment is like the meeting of two baboons; and when a man thanks me heartily, it feels as if I've given him a penny and he's paying me back the beggarly thanks. Come on, sing—and those of you who won't, hold your tongues.

6.13.oldText: AMIENS. All right, I'll finish the song. Sirs, set the table meanwhile; the Duke will drink under this tree. He's been looking for you all day.

6.14.oldText: JAQUES. And I've been avoiding him all day. He's too argumentative for my company. I think about as many things as he does; but I thank heaven and don't boast about them. Come on, warble away.

6.17.oldText: Whoever shuns ambition, And loves to live in the sun, Seeking the food he eats, And pleased with what he gets, Come hither, come hither, come hither. Here he shall see No enemy But winter and rough weather.

6.18.oldText: JAQUES. I'll give you a verse for this tune that I made yesterday in spite of my own creativity.

6.21.oldText: If it should come to pass That any man turns ass, Leaving his wealth and ease A stubborn will to please, Ducdame, ducdame, ducdame; Here he shall see Gross fools just like he, If he'll come over to me.

6.23.oldText: JAQUES. It's a Greek invocation, to call fools into a circle. I'll go sleep, if I can; if I can't, I'll rant against all the first-born of Egypt.

6.24.oldText: AMIENS. And I'll go find the Duke; his banquet is ready. Exeunt severally

7.2.oldText: ADAM. Dear master, I can't go any further. Oh, I'm dying for food! I'll lie down here and mark out my grave. Farewell, kind master.

7.3.oldText: ORLANDO. Why, what's this, Adam! No greater heart than that in you? Live a little; take a little comfort; cheer yourself a little. If this rough forest contains anything wild, I'll either be food for it or bring it back as food for you. Your imagination is nearer death than your strength is. For my sake, be brave; hold death off a little longer, at arm's length. I'll be back with you shortly; and if I don't bring you something to eat, I'll give you permission to die. But if you die before I come back, you're mocking my efforts. Well said! You're looking cheerful. I'll be with you quickly. But you're lying out in the bleak air. Come, I'll carry you to some shelter; and you shall not die for lack of a dinner, if anything alive exists in this wilderness. Cheer up, good Adam! Exeunt

8.1.oldText: A table set out. Enter DUKE SENIOR, AMIENS, and LORDS, like outlaws

8.2.oldText: DUKE SENIOR. I think he must have been transformed into a beast; For nowhere can I find him in the shape of a man.

8.3.oldText: FIRST LORD. My lord, he just now left this spot; He was here merrily, listening to a song.

8.4.oldText: DUKE SENIOR. If he, who's made of discord, grows musical, We'll soon have discord in the music of the spheres. Go find him; tell him I would speak with him.

8.6.oldText: FIRST LORD. He saves me the trouble by coming on his own.

8.7.oldText: DUKE SENIOR. Why, what's this, monsieur! What kind of life is this, That your poor friends must beg for your company? What, you look merry!

8.8.oldText: JAQUES. A fool, a fool! I met a fool in the forest, A motley fool. A miserable world! As I live by food, I met a fool, Who laid himself down and basked in the sun, And railed at Lady Fortune in good terms, In well-formed terms—and yet a motley fool. 'Good morning, fool,' I said. 'No, sir,' he answered, 'Don't call me fool till heaven has sent me fortune.' And then he drew a sundial from his pouch, And, looking at it with a dull eye, Says very wisely, 'It is ten o'clock. Thus we may see,' he said, 'how the world wags. It's only an hour since it was nine; And after one hour more it will be eleven; And so, from hour to hour, we ripe and ripe, And then, from hour to hour, we rot and rot; And thereby hangs a tale.' When I heard The motley fool moralize like that on time, My lungs began to crow like a rooster That fools should be so deeply contemplative; And I laughed without stop For an hour by his dial. Oh, noble fool! A worthy fool! Motley is the only thing to wear.

8.9.oldText: DUKE SENIOR. What fool is this?

8.10.oldText: JAQUES. Oh, worthy fool! One who has been a courtier, And says that if ladies are only young and fair, They have the gift to know it. And in his brain, Which is as dry as the leftover biscuit After a voyage, he has strange places crammed With observation, which he gives out In mangled forms. Oh, that I were a fool! I'm ambitious for a motley coat.

8.11.oldText: DUKE SENIOR. You shall have one.

8.12.oldText: JAQUES. It is the only suit I want, Provided you weed your better judgments Of every opinion that has grown rank in them That I am wise. I must have liberty along with it— As large a charter as the wind, To blow on whom I please, for so fools do; And those who are most galled by my folly Must laugh the loudest. And why, sir, must they do so? The reason is plain as the path to the parish church: He whom a fool very wisely hits Acts very foolishly, although it stings him, Not to seem insensible of the blow. If he doesn't, The wise man's folly is anatomized Even by the random glances of the fool. Dress me in my motley; give me leave To speak my mind, and I will, through and through, Cleanse the foul body of this infected world, If they'll patiently receive my medicine.

8.13.oldText: DUKE SENIOR. Shame on you! I can tell what you'd do.

8.14.oldText: JAQUES. What, for a counter, would I do but good?
