8.15.oldText: DUKE SENIOR. The most mischievous, foul sin of all—scolding sin. For you yourself have been a libertine, As sensual as the brutish sting itself; And all the swollen sores and headed evils That you with free license have caught, You would now disgorge into the wider world.

8.16.oldText: JAQUES. Why, who cries out against pride That can therein accuse any private person? Doesn't it flow as hugely as the sea, Till the wearer's very means ebb dry? What woman in the city do I name When I say the city-woman bears The cost of princes on unworthy shoulders? Who can come in and say I mean her, When her neighbor is just such another? Or what man of the basest occupation Is there, who says his finery isn't bought with my cost, Thinking I mean him, but in doing so fits His folly to the mettle of my speech? There then! How then? What then? Let me see how My tongue has wronged him: if it does him right, Then he has wronged himself; if he is innocent, Why, then my accusation flies like a wild goose, Claimed by no man. But who's coming here?

8.17.oldText: Enter ORLANDO with his sword drawn

8.18.oldText: ORLANDO. Stop, and eat no more.

8.19.oldText: JAQUES. Why, I haven't eaten any yet.

8.20.oldText: ORLANDO. Nor shall you, until necessity is served.

8.21.oldText: JAQUES. What kind of rooster does this one come from?

8.22.oldText: DUKE SENIOR. Are you made this bold, man, by your distress? Or are you a rude despiser of good manners, That you seem so empty of civility?

8.23.oldText: ORLANDO. You touched my vein at the first: the thorny point Of bare distress has stripped from me the show Of smooth civility. Yet I was brought up inland, And know some good breeding. But stop, I say; Anyone who touches any of this fruit dies Until I and my affairs are answered.

8.24.oldText: JAQUES. If you won't be answered with reason, then I must die.

8.25.oldText: DUKE SENIOR. What do you want? Your gentleness will compel More than your force will move us to gentleness.

8.26.oldText: ORLANDO. I'm almost dying for food, so let me have some.

8.27.oldText: DUKE SENIOR. Sit down and eat, and welcome to our table.

8.28.oldText: ORLANDO. Do you speak so gently? Pardon me, please; I thought all things here were savage, And so I put on the countenance Of stern command. But whoever you are That in this inaccessible wilderness, Under the shade of melancholy boughs, Lose and neglect the creeping hours of time; If you've ever known better days, If you've ever been where bells have rung for church, If you've ever sat at any good man's feast, If you've ever wiped a tear from your eyelid, And know what it is to pity and be pitied, Let gentleness be my strong enforcement; In hope of which I blush, and hide my sword.

8.29.oldText: DUKE SENIOR. It's true we've seen better days, And have been called to church by holy bell, And sat at good men's feasts, and wiped our eyes Of drops that sacred pity has engendered; And so sit down in gentleness, And take by request whatever help we have That can be ministered to your need.

8.30.oldText: ORLANDO. Then only hold back your food a little while, While, like a doe, I go to find my fawn, And give him food. There is an old poor man Who has, after me, in pure love Limped many a weary step. Till he is first satisfied, Oppressed by two weak evils, age and hunger, I will not touch a bite.

8.31.oldText: DUKE SENIOR. Go and find him. And we will waste nothing until you return.

8.32.oldText: ORLANDO. I thank you, and be blessed for your good comfort! Exit

8.33.oldText: DUKE SENIOR. You see we aren't alone in being unhappy: This wide and universal theater Presents more woeful pageants than the scene We play in.

8.34.oldText: JAQUES. All the world's a stage, And all the men and women merely players; They have their exits and their entrances, And one man in his time plays many parts, His acts being seven ages. At first the infant, Mewling and puking in the nurse's arms; Then the whining schoolboy, with his satchel And shining morning face, creeping like a snail Unwillingly to school. And then the lover, Sighing like a furnace, with a woeful ballad Made to his mistress's eyebrow. Then a soldier, Full of strange oaths and bearded like the leopard, Jealous in honor, sudden and quick to quarrel, Seeking the bubble reputation Even in the cannon's mouth. And then the justice, With fair round belly lined with good capon, With severe eyes and beard of formal cut, Full of wise sayings and modern examples; And so he plays his part. The sixth age shifts Into the lean and slippered pantaloon, With spectacles on his nose and pouch at his side; His youthful hose, well saved, a world too wide For his shrunken shank; and his big manly voice, Turning again toward childish treble, pipes And whistles in its sound. Last scene of all, That ends this strange eventful history, Is second childishness and mere oblivion— Sans teeth, sans eyes, sans taste, sans everything.

8.36.oldText: DUKE SENIOR. Welcome. Set down your venerable burden, And let him eat.

8.37.oldText: ORLANDO. I thank you most on his behalf.

8.38.oldText: ADAM. As well you should; I can scarcely speak to thank you for myself.

8.39.oldText: DUKE SENIOR. Welcome; fall to. I won't trouble you As yet to ask about your fortunes. Give us some music; and, good cousin, sing.

8.40.oldText: SONG Blow, blow, you winter wind, You are not so unkind As man's ingratitude; Your tooth is not so keen, Because you are not seen, Although your breath be rough. Heigh-ho! sing heigh-ho! unto the green holly. Most friendship is feigning, most loving mere folly. Then, heigh-ho, the holly! This life is most jolly.

8.41.oldText: Freeze, freeze, you bitter sky, That do not bite so near As benefits forgot; Though you warp the waters, Your sting is not so sharp As a friend remembered not. Heigh-ho! sing, &c.

8.42.oldText: DUKE SENIOR. If you were the good Sir Rowland's son, As you have whispered faithfully you are, And as my eye does witness his likeness Most truly drawn and living in your face, Be truly welcome here. I am the Duke That loved your father. The rest of your story, Come to my cave and tell me. Good old man, You are right welcome, as your master is. Support him by the arm. Give me your hand, And let me understand all your fortunes. Exeunt

8.44.oldText: Enter DUKE FREDERICK, OLIVER, and LORDS

8.45.oldText: FREDERICK. Not seen him since! Sir, sir, that cannot be. But were I not made more of mercy than anything else, I wouldn't seek an absent target For my revenge while you are present. But see to it: Find out your brother wherever he is; Search him out with a candle; bring him back dead or living Within this twelvemonth, or never come back yourself To seek a living in our territory. Your lands and all things that you call yours Worth seizing we do seize into our hands, Until you can clear yourself by your brother's word Of what we think against you.

8.46.oldText: OLIVER. Oh, if only your Highness knew my heart in this! I never loved my brother in my life.

8.47.oldText: FREDERICK. The greater villain you. Well, push him out the doors; And let my officers of that kind Make an inventory of his house and lands. Do this with dispatch, and send him on his way. Exeunt

9.2.oldText: ORLANDO. Hang there, my verse, as witness of my love; And you, thrice-crowned Queen of the Night, survey With your chaste eye, from your pale sphere above, Your huntress's name that rules my whole life. O Rosalind! these trees shall be my books, And in their barks I'll inscribe my thoughts, So that every eye that looks in this forest Shall see your virtue witnessed everywhere. Run, run, Orlando; carve on every tree The fair, the chaste, the inexpressible she. Exit

9.4.oldText: CORIN. And how do you like this shepherd's life, Master Touchstone?

9.5.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. Truly, shepherd, in itself it's a good life; but inasmuch as it is a shepherd's life, it is nothing. Inasmuch as it is solitary, I like it very well; but inasmuch as it is private, it's a very vile life. Now inasmuch as it's in the fields, it pleases me well; but inasmuch as it is not at court, it's tedious. As it is a simple life, you see, it suits my mood well; but as there is no more abundance in it, it goes much against my stomach. Have you any philosophy in you, shepherd?

9.6.oldText: CORIN. No more than that I know: the more sick a man is, the worse off he is; and that he who lacks money, means, and contentment lacks three good friends; that the property of rain is to wet, and fire to burn; that good pasture makes fat sheep; and that a great cause of night is lack of the sun; that he who has learned no wit by nature or by art may complain about his upbringing, or else he comes from very dull kin.

9.7.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. Such a one is a natural philosopher. Have you ever been at court, shepherd?

9.11.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. Truly, you are damned, like an ill-roasted egg, all on one side.

9.12.oldText: CORIN. For not being at court? Give me your reason.

9.13.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. Why, if you were never at court, you never saw good manners; if you never saw good manners, then your manners must be wicked; and wickedness is sin, and sin is damnation. You're in a perilous state, shepherd.

9.14.oldText: CORIN. Not a bit, Touchstone. Those things that count as good manners at court are as ridiculous in the country as the behavior of the country is most mockable at court. You told me that at court you don't bow but kiss your hands. That kind of courtesy would be unclean if courtiers were shepherds.

9.15.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. An example, briefly; come, an example.

9.16.oldText: CORIN. Well, we are always handling our ewes, and their fleeces, you know, are greasy.

9.17.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. Why, don't courtiers' hands sweat? And isn't the grease of a sheep as wholesome as the sweat of a man? Shallow, shallow. A better example, I say; come on.

9.18.oldText: CORIN. Besides, our hands are hard.

9.19.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. Your lips will feel them all the sooner. Shallow again. A sounder example; come.

9.20.oldText: CORIN. And they are often tarred over from doctoring our sheep; and would you have us kiss tar? Courtiers' hands are perfumed with civet.

9.21.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. Most shallow man! You're worm's-meat compared to a good piece of flesh, indeed! Learn from the wise, and consider: civet is of a baser birth than tar—the very uncleanly discharge of a cat. Improve your example, shepherd.

9.22.oldText: CORIN. You have too courtly a wit for me; I'll give up.

9.23.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. Will you give up and be damned? God help you, shallow man! God make an incision in you! You are raw.

9.24.oldText: CORIN. Sir, I am a true laborer: I earn what I eat, get what I wear; owe no man hate, envy no man's happiness; glad of other men's good, content with my own harm; and the greatest pride I have is to see my ewes graze and my lambs suck.

9.25.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. That is another simple sin in you: to bring the ewes and the rams together, and to make your living by the copulation of livestock; to be pimp to a bellwether, and to betray a year-old female lamb to a crooked-headed, old, cuckoldly ram, totally unsuited to her. If you aren't damned for this, the devil himself will have no shepherds; I can't see otherwise how you can escape.

9.26.oldText: CORIN. Here comes young Master Ganymede, my new mistress's brother.

9.28.oldText: ROSALIND. 'From the east to the western Indies, No jewel is like Rosalind. Her worth, being carried on the wind, Through all the world bears the name of Rosalind. All the pictures most beautifully drawn Are but dark beside Rosalind. Let no face be kept in mind But the fairness of Rosalind.'

9.29.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. I could rhyme you like that for eight years straight, leaving out only dinners, suppers, and sleeping hours. It's the regular butter-women's plodding rhythm to market.

9.31.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. For a sample: If a hart should lack a hind, Let him seek out Rosalind. If the cat will mate in kind, So as surely will Rosalind. Winter garments must be lined, So must slender Rosalind. They that reap must sheaf and bind, Then to cart with Rosalind. Sweetest nut has sourest rind, Such a nut is Rosalind. He that the sweetest rose will find Must find love's thorn and Rosalind. This is the very false gallop of verses; why are you infecting yourself with them?

9.32.oldText: ROSALIND. Quiet, you dull fool! I found them on a tree.

9.33.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. Truly, the tree yields bad fruit.

9.34.oldText: ROSALIND. I'll graft it with you, and then I'll graft it with a medlar. Then it will produce the earliest fruit in the country; for you'll be rotten before you're half ripe, and that's the special quality of the medlar.

9.35.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. You have spoken; but whether wisely or not, let the forest judge.

9.37.oldText: ROSALIND. Quiet! Here comes my sister, reading; stand aside.

9.38.oldText: CELIA. 'Why should this be a desert? Because it is unpeopled? No; I'll hang tongues on every tree That shall reveal civil sayings. Some, about how brief the life of man Runs his erring pilgrimage, And that the stretch of a hand-span Buckles in the sum of his age; Some, about violated vows Between the souls of friend and friend; But upon the fairest boughs, Or at every sentence end, I will write 'Rosalinda,' Teaching all who read to know The quintessence of every spirit That heaven would in little show. Therefore heaven charged Nature That one body should be filled With all graces widely spread. Nature immediately distilled Helen's cheek, but not her heart, Cleopatra's majesty, Atalanta's better part, Sad Lucretia's modesty. Thus Rosalind of many parts By heavenly synod was devised, Of many faces, eyes, and hearts, To have the touches most dearly prized. Heaven willed that she should have these gifts, And I, to live and die her slave.'

9.39.oldText: ROSALIND. O most gentle Jupiter! What a tedious sermon of love you've wearied your parishioners with—and never cried 'Have patience, good people.'

9.40.oldText: CELIA. What now! Back, friends—shepherd, step off a bit; go with him, sirrah.

9.41.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. Come, shepherd, let us make an honorable retreat;

9.42.oldText: though not with bag and baggage, yet with knapsack and contents. Exeunt CORIN and TOUCHSTONE

9.43.oldText: CELIA. Did you hear those verses?

9.44.oldText: ROSALIND. Oh yes, I heard them all, and more besides—because some of them had more feet than the verses could bear.

9.45.oldText: CELIA. That's no matter; the feet might bear up the verses.

9.46.oldText: ROSALIND. Yes, but the feet were lame, and couldn't bear themselves without the verse, and so they stood lamely in the verse.

9.47.oldText: CELIA. But did you hear without wondering how your name comes to be hanging and carved upon these trees?

9.48.oldText: ROSALIND. I was seven of the nine days out of wondering before you came; for look here what I found on a palm-tree. I haven't been so rhymed at since Pythagoras' time, when I was an Irish rat—which I can hardly remember.

9.49.oldText: CELIA. Can you guess who has done this?

9.51.oldText: CELIA. And with a chain about his neck that you once wore. Are you changing color?

9.53.oldText: CELIA. O Lord, Lord! It's a hard thing for friends to meet; but mountains may be moved by earthquakes, and so encounter each other.

9.54.oldText: ROSALIND. No, but who is it?

9.56.oldText: ROSALIND. No, please, now, with the most petitionary vehemence, tell me who it is.

9.57.oldText: CELIA. Oh wonderful, wonderful, most wonderful wonderful, and yet again wonderful, and beyond all whooping!

9.58.oldText: ROSALIND. Mercy on my complexion! Do you think, just because I'm dressed up like a man, I have a doublet and hose in my temperament too? One inch more of delay is a South Sea of discovery. Please tell me who it is, quickly, and speak fast. I wish you could stammer, so you could pour this concealed man out of your mouth, as wine comes out of a narrow-mouthed bottle—either too much at once or none at all. Please, take the cork out of your mouth so I can drink your tidings.

9.59.oldText: CELIA. So you can put a man inside your belly.

9.60.oldText: ROSALIND. Is he of God's making? What kind of man? Is his head worth a hat or his chin worth a beard?

9.61.oldText: CELIA. No, he has only a little beard.

9.62.oldText: ROSALIND. Why, God will send more if the man will be thankful. I'll wait for his beard to grow, so long as you don't make me wait for the news of his chin.

9.63.oldText: CELIA. It is young Orlando, who tripped up the wrestler's heels and your heart both in the same instant.

9.64.oldText: ROSALIND. No, but the devil take mocking! Speak with a serious brow and as a truthful maid.

9.65.oldText: CELIA. In faith, cousin, it's him.

9.68.oldText: ROSALIND. Alas the day! What shall I do with my doublet and hose? What was he doing when you saw him? What did he say? How did he look? What was he wearing? What's he doing here? Did he ask for me? Where's he staying? How did he take leave of you? And when will you see him again? Answer me in one word.

9.69.oldText: CELIA. First you must lend me Gargantua's mouth; that's a word too big for any mouth of this age's size. To say yes and no to all these particulars is more than answering a catechism.

9.70.oldText: ROSALIND. But does he know that I am in this forest, and in man's clothing? Does he look as fresh as he did the day he wrestled?

9.71.oldText: CELIA. It's as easy to count motes of dust as to settle the questions of a lover. But have a taste of how I found him, and savor it with attention. I found him under a tree, like a dropped acorn.

9.72.oldText: ROSALIND. It may well be called Jove's tree, when it drops such fruit.

9.73.oldText: CELIA. Hear me out, good madam.

9.75.oldText: CELIA. There he lay, stretched out like a wounded knight.

9.76.oldText: ROSALIND. Though it's a pity to see such a sight, it suits the ground well.

9.77.oldText: CELIA. Cry 'Whoa' to your tongue, please; it's prancing out of season. He was outfitted like a hunter.

9.78.oldText: ROSALIND. Oh, ominous! He comes to kill my heart.

9.79.oldText: CELIA. I'd like to sing my song without an interruption; you're throwing me off-key.

9.80.oldText: ROSALIND. Don't you know I am a woman? When I think, I must speak. Sweet, go on.

9.81.oldText: CELIA. You're putting me off. Soft! Isn't that him coming here?

9.83.oldText: ROSALIND. It's him. Slink by, and watch him.

9.84.oldText: JAQUES. I thank you for your company; but in good faith, I'd just as soon have been alone.

9.85.oldText: ORLANDO. And so would I; but yet, for fashion's sake, I thank you also for your company.

9.86.oldText: JAQUES. God be with you; let's meet as little as we can.

9.87.oldText: ORLANDO. I do wish we may be better strangers.

9.88.oldText: JAQUES. Please, mar no more trees by writing love songs in their barks.

9.89.oldText: ORLANDO. Please, mar no more of my verses by reading them so badly.

9.90.oldText: JAQUES. Rosalind is your love's name?

9.92.oldText: JAQUES. I don't like her name.

9.93.oldText: ORLANDO. There was no thought of pleasing you when she was christened.

9.95.oldText: ORLANDO. Just as high as my heart.

9.96.oldText: JAQUES. You are full of pretty answers. Haven't you been hanging around with goldsmiths' wives, and memorized them off rings?

9.97.oldText: ORLANDO. Not so; rather, I answer you straight from painted cloth, from which you have studied your questions.

9.98.oldText: JAQUES. You have a nimble wit; I think it was made from Atalanta's heels. Will you sit down with me? And we two will rail against our mistress the world, and all our misery.

9.99.oldText: ORLANDO. I will scold no living creature in the world but myself, against whom I know the most faults.

9.100.oldText: JAQUES. The worst fault you have is being in love.

9.101.oldText: ORLANDO. That's a fault I would not exchange for your best virtue. I'm weary of you.

9.102.oldText: JAQUES. By my faith, I was looking for a fool when I found you.

9.103.oldText: ORLANDO. He's drowned in the brook; just look in, and you'll see him.

9.104.oldText: JAQUES. There I shall see my own figure.

9.105.oldText: ORLANDO. Which I take to be either a fool or a zero.

9.106.oldText: JAQUES. I'll stay no longer with you. Farewell, good Signior Love.

9.107.oldText: ORLANDO. I'm glad of your departure; adieu, good Monsieur Melancholy. Exit JAQUES

9.108.oldText: ROSALIND. [Aside to CELIA] I'll speak to him like a saucy lackey, and under that disguise play the knave with him.—Do you hear, forester?

9.109.oldText: ORLANDO. Very well; what do you want?

9.110.oldText: ROSALIND. Please, what time is it?

9.111.oldText: ORLANDO. You should ask me what time of day it is; there's no clock in the forest.

9.112.oldText: ROSALIND. Then there's no true lover in the forest, since sighing every minute and groaning every hour would detect the lazy foot of Time as well as a clock.

9.113.oldText: ORLANDO. And why not the swift foot of Time? Wouldn't that have been as proper?

9.114.oldText: ROSALIND. By no means, sir. Time travels at different paces with different people. I'll tell you with whom Time ambles, with whom Time trots, with whom Time gallops, and with whom he stands still.

9.115.oldText: ORLANDO. Please, with whom does he trot?

9.116.oldText: ROSALIND. Why, he trots hard with a young maid between the contract of her marriage and the day it is solemnized. If the interval is only a week, Time's pace is so hard that it seems the length of seven years.

9.117.oldText: ORLANDO. With whom does Time amble?

9.118.oldText: ROSALIND. With a priest who lacks Latin and a rich man who hasn't got the gout; the one sleeps easily because he can't study, and the other lives merrily because he feels no pain; the one lacking the burden of lean and wasteful learning, the other knowing no burden of heavy tedious poverty. With these two Time ambles.

9.119.oldText: ORLANDO. With whom does he gallop?

9.120.oldText: ROSALIND. With a thief on his way to the gallows; for though he goes as softly as foot can fall, he thinks himself there too soon.

9.121.oldText: ORLANDO. With whom does he stand still?

9.122.oldText: ROSALIND. With lawyers during the vacation; for they sleep between term and term, and so they don't perceive how Time moves.

9.123.oldText: ORLANDO. Where do you live, pretty youth?

9.124.oldText: ROSALIND. With this shepherdess, my sister; here on the outskirts of the forest, like fringe on a petticoat.

9.125.oldText: ORLANDO. Are you native to this place?

9.126.oldText: ROSALIND. As is the rabbit that you see live where she's born.

9.127.oldText: ROSALIND. Your accent is somewhat finer than you could have acquired in such a remote dwelling.

9.128.oldText: ROSALIND. So I have been told by many; but indeed, an old religious uncle of mine taught me to speak. He was in his youth an inland man—one who knew courtship too well, for there he fell in love. I've heard him read many lectures against it; and I thank God I am not a woman, to be tainted with so many giddy offenses as he generally charged their whole sex with.

9.129.oldText: ORLANDO. Can you remember any of the principal evils he laid to women's charge?

9.130.oldText: ROSALIND. There were no principal ones; they were all like one another the way halfpennies are; every fault seemed monstrous till its fellow-fault came along to match it.

9.131.oldText: ORLANDO. Please recount some of them.

9.132.oldText: ROSALIND. No; I won't waste my medicine on any but the sick. There's a man who haunts the forest abusing our young plants by carving 'Rosalind' on their barks; hanging odes upon hawthorns and elegies on brambles—all, indeed, deifying the name of Rosalind. If I could meet that fancy-monger, I'd give him some good counsel, for he seems to have the daily fever of love upon him.

9.133.oldText: ORLANDO. I am the one so love-shaken; please tell me your remedy.

9.134.oldText: ROSALIND. There's none of my uncle's marks upon you; he taught me how to recognize a man in love; and you, I'm sure, are not a prisoner in that cage of rushes.

9.136.oldText: ROSALIND. A lean cheek, which you don't have; a blue, sunken eye, which you don't have; an unquestionable spirit, which you don't have; a neglected beard, which you don't have—but I pardon you for that, since what little beard you have is a younger brother's revenue. Then your hose should be ungartered, your bonnet without a band, your sleeve unbuttoned, your shoe untied, and everything about you showing a careless desolation. But you are no such man; you're rather point-perfect in your dress, looking like a lover of yourself rather than a lover of anyone else.

9.137.oldText: ORLANDO. Fair youth, I wish I could make you believe I am in love.

9.138.oldText: ROSALIND. Me believe it! You may as soon make her that you love believe it; which, I assure you, she's quicker to do than to confess she does. That's one of the points on which women still give the lie to their consciences. But, truly now, are you the one who hangs the verses on the trees in which Rosalind is so admired?

9.139.oldText: ORLANDO. I swear to you, youth, by the white hand of Rosalind, I am he—that unfortunate he.

9.140.oldText: ROSALIND. But are you really as much in love as your rhymes say?

9.141.oldText: ORLANDO. Neither rhyme nor reason can express how much.

9.142.oldText: ROSALIND. Love is merely a madness; and, I tell you, it deserves a dark house and a whip as much as madmen do. The reason they aren't so punished and cured is that the lunacy is so common that the whippers are in love too. Yet I claim to cure it by counsel.

9.143.oldText: ORLANDO. Did you ever cure any so?

9.144.oldText: ROSALIND. Yes, one; and in this way. He was to imagine me his love, his mistress; and I set him every day to woo me. At which times I, being but a moonish youth, would grieve, be effeminate, changeable, longing and liking, proud, fantastical, apish, shallow, inconstant, full of tears, full of smiles—for every passion something, and for no passion truly anything, as boys and women are for the most part creatures of this stripe. I'd now like him, now loathe him; then entertain him, then forswear him; now weep for him, then spit at him—so I drove my suitor from his mad humor of love into a living humor of madness, which was to forswear the full stream of the world and to live in a corner merely monastic. And thus I cured him; and this way I'll undertake to wash your liver as clean as a sound sheep's heart, so there shall not be one spot of love in it.

9.145.oldText: ORLANDO. I would not be cured, youth.

9.146.oldText: ROSALIND. I would cure you, if you would just call me Rosalind, and come every day to my cottage and woo me.

9.147.oldText: ORLANDO. Now, by the faith of my love, I will. Tell me where it is.

9.148.oldText: ROSALIND. Come with me to it, and I'll show you; and on the way, you can tell me where in the forest you live. Will you come?

9.149.oldText: ORLANDO. With all my heart, good youth.

9.150.oldText: ROSALIND. No, you must call me Rosalind. Come, sister, will you come? Exeunt

10.1.oldText: Enter TOUCHSTONE and AUDREY; JAQUES behind

10.2.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. Come along quickly, good Audrey; I'll fetch up your goats, Audrey. And how about it, Audrey—am I the man yet? Does my simple appearance content you?

10.3.oldText: AUDREY. Your features! Lord protect us! What features?

10.4.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. I am here with you and your goats, just as the most capricious poet, honest Ovid, was among the Goths.

10.5.oldText: JAQUES. [Aside] Oh, knowledge poorly housed, worse than Jove in a thatched cottage!

10.6.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. When a man's verses can't be understood, nor a man's good wit backed up by the forward child Understanding, it strikes a man deader than a great bill in a little room. Truly, I wish the gods had made you poetical.

10.7.oldText: AUDREY. I don't know what 'poetical' is. Is it honest in deed and word? Is it a true thing?

10.8.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. No, truly; the truest poetry is the most feigning, and lovers are given to poetry; and what they swear in poetry may be said, as lovers, they only feign.

10.9.oldText: AUDREY. Do you wish, then, that the gods had made me poetical?

10.10.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. I do, truly, because you swear to me you are honest. Now, if you were a poet, I might have some hope you were faking.

10.11.oldText: AUDREY. Wouldn't you have me honest?

10.12.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. No, truly, unless you were ugly. For honesty coupled with beauty is like having honey as a sauce for sugar.

10.14.oldText: AUDREY. Well, I'm not pretty; and so I pray the gods to make me honest.

10.15.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. Truly, and to throw away honesty on a foul slut would be to put good meat into an unclean dish.

10.16.oldText: AUDREY. I am not a slut, though I thank the gods I am foul.

10.17.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. Well, praised be the gods for your foulness; sluttishness may come hereafter. But be it as it may, I'll marry you. And to that end I have been with Sir Oliver Martext, the vicar of the next village, who has promised to meet me here in this place in the forest and join us together.

10.18.oldText: JAQUES. [Aside] I'd love to see this meeting.

10.19.oldText: AUDREY. Well, may the gods give us joy!

10.20.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. Amen. A man might, if he had a fearful heart, hesitate at this attempt; for here we have no temple but the wood, no assembly but horned beasts. But what of it? Courage! As horns are odious, they are necessary. It is said: 'Many a man knows no end of his goods.' Right! Many a man has good horns and knows no end of them. Well, those are his wife's dowry; they're none of his own getting. Horns? Just so. Only on poor men? No, no; the noblest deer has them as huge as the rascal. Is the single man therefore blessed? No; as a walled town is more worthy than a village, so is the forehead of a married man more honorable than the bare brow of a bachelor. And by as much as defense is better than no skill, by so much is having a horn more precious than to lack one. Here comes Sir Oliver.

10.22.oldText: Sir Oliver Martext, well met. Will you dispatch us here under this tree, or shall we go with you to your chapel?

10.23.oldText: MARTEXT. Is there no one here to give the woman away?

10.24.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. I won't take her as a gift from any man.

10.25.oldText: MARTEXT. Truly, she must be given away, or the marriage isn't lawful.

10.26.oldText: JAQUES. [Discovering himself] Proceed, proceed; I'll give her away.

10.27.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. Good evening, good Master What-do-you-call-him; how are you, sir? You're well met. God reward you for your last company. I'm very glad to see you. Just a trifle in hand here, sir. No; please, keep your hat on.

10.28.oldText: JAQUES. Will you be married, motley?

10.29.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. As the ox has his yoke, sir, the horse his curb, and the falcon her bells, so man has his desires; and as pigeons bill, so wedlock would be nibbling.

10.30.oldText: JAQUES. And will you, being a man of your breeding, be married under a bush, like a beggar? Get yourself to a church and find a good priest who can tell you what marriage is. This fellow will only join you together as they join wainscot; then one of you will prove to be a shrunk panel, and like green timber, warp, warp.

10.31.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. [Aside] I'm of a mind that I'm better off married by him than by another. He's not likely to marry me well, and not being well married will be a good excuse for me hereafter to leave my wife.

10.32.oldText: JAQUES. Come along with me, and let me counsel you.

10.33.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. Come, sweet Audrey; We must be married, or we must live in vice. Farewell, good Master Oliver. Not— O sweet Oliver, O brave Oliver, Leave me not behind you. But— Be off, Begone, I say, I will not go to wedding with you. Exeunt JAQUES, TOUCHSTONE, and AUDREY

10.34.oldText: MARTEXT. No matter; not one fantastical knave among them all shall mock me out of my calling. Exit

11.2.oldText: ROSALIND. Don't talk to me; I'm going to weep.

11.3.oldText: CELIA. Do, please; but yet have the grace to consider that tears don't become a man.

11.4.oldText: ROSALIND. But haven't I cause to weep?

11.5.oldText: CELIA. As good a cause as anyone could want; so weep.

11.6.oldText: ROSALIND. His very hair is of the deceiving color.

11.7.oldText: CELIA. Something browner than Judas's. Marry, his kisses are Judas's own children.

11.8.oldText: ROSALIND. By my faith, his hair is of a good color.

11.9.oldText: CELIA. An excellent color: your chestnut was always the only color.

11.10.oldText: ROSALIND. And his kissing is as full of sanctity as the touch of holy bread.

11.11.oldText: CELIA. He has bought a pair of cast-off lips from Diana. A nun of the winter sisterhood doesn't kiss more religiously; the very ice of chastity is in them.

11.12.oldText: ROSALIND. But why did he swear he would come this morning, and isn't here?

11.13.oldText: CELIA. No, certainly, there is no truth in him.

11.15.oldText: CELIA. Yes; I think he's not a pickpurse or a horse-thief; but for his truthfulness in love, I think him as hollow as a covered goblet or a worm-eaten nut.

11.17.oldText: CELIA. Yes, when he is in love; but I don't think he's in.

11.18.oldText: ROSALIND. You heard him swear flat out that he was.

11.19.oldText: CELIA. 'Was' is not 'is'; besides, the oath of a lover is no stronger than the word of a tavern-keeper; they're both confirmers of false reckonings. He attends here in the forest on the Duke, your father.

11.20.oldText: ROSALIND. I met the Duke yesterday, and had much conversation with him. He asked me of what parentage I was. I told him, of as good as his; so he laughed and let me go. But what are we talking about fathers for, when there's such a man as Orlando?

11.21.oldText: CELIA. Oh, that's a brave man! He writes brave verses, speaks brave words, swears brave oaths, and breaks them bravely—quite athwart, sideways across the heart of his lover; like a puny jouster who spurs his horse on only one side, and breaks his staff like a noble goose. But all things are brave that youth mounts and folly guides. Who's coming here?

11.23.oldText: CORIN. Mistress and master, you have often inquired After the shepherd who complained of love, Whom you saw sitting by me on the turf, Praising the proud and disdainful shepherdess Who was his mistress.

11.24.oldText: CELIA. Well, and what of him?

11.25.oldText: CORIN. If you would like to see a pageant truly played Between the pale complexion of true love And the red glow of scorn and proud disdain, Come a little way from here, and I'll conduct you, If you'd like to observe.

11.26.oldText: ROSALIND. Oh, come, let's go! The sight of lovers feeds those who are in love. Bring us to this sight, and you'll say I'll play a busy actor in their play. Exeunt

12.2.oldText: SILVIUS. Sweet Phebe, do not scorn me; do not, Phebe. Say that you do not love me; but do not say it In bitterness. The common executioner, Whose heart the accustomed sight of death makes hard, Does not let the axe fall upon the humbled neck Without first begging pardon. Will you be sterner Than he who lives and dies by bloody drops?

12.3.oldText: Enter ROSALIND, CELIA, and CORIN, at a distance

12.4.oldText: PHEBE. I would not be your executioner; I flee from you, because I would not injure you. You tell me there is murder in my eye. That's a pretty notion, surely, and very probable, That eyes—which are the most fragile and softest things, Which shut their cowardly gates against motes of dust— Should be called tyrants, butchers, murderers! Now I do frown on you with all my heart; And if my eyes can wound, now let them kill you. Now pretend to swoon; why, now fall down; Or if you cannot, oh, for shame, for shame, Do not lie and say my eyes are murderers. Now show me the wound my eye has made in you. Scratch yourself with a pin and there remains Some scar of it; lean upon a rush, And the imprint and visible impression Your palm keeps for a moment; but now my eyes, Which I have darted at you, hurt you not; Nor, I am sure, is there force in eyes That can do hurt.

12.5.oldText: SILVIUS. Oh dear Phebe, If ever—and that may be near at hand— You meet in some fresh cheek the power of love, Then you shall know the wounds invisible That love's keen arrows make.

12.6.oldText: PHEBE. But till that time Don't come near me; and when that time comes, Afflict me with your mockery, do not pity me; As until that time, I shall not pity you.

12.7.oldText: ROSALIND. [Advancing] And why, please tell me? Who might be your mother, That you insult, exult, and all at once, Over the wretched? What though you have no beauty— For, by my faith, I see no more in you Than someone might see going to bed in the dark without a candle— Must you therefore be proud and pitiless? Why, what does this mean? Why do you look at me? I see no more in you than in the ordinary Sale-work of nature. By my life, I think she means to tangle my eyes too! No, faith, proud mistress, don't hope for it; It is not your inky brows, your black silk hair, Your bead-like eyeballs, nor your cheek of cream That can tame my spirit into worshiping you. You foolish shepherd, why do you follow her, Like the foggy south, puffing with wind and rain? You are a thousand times more proper a man Than she is a woman. It is such fools as you That make the world full of ill-favored children. It is not her mirror, but you, that flatters her; And out of you she sees herself more proper Than any of her features can show her. But, mistress, know yourself. Down on your knees, And thank heaven, fasting, for a good man's love; For I must tell you, friendly in your ear: Sell when you can; you are not for all markets. Beg the man's mercy, love him, take his offer; Foul is most foul, being foul, to be a scoffer. So, take her to yourself, shepherd. Fare you well.

12.8.oldText: PHEBE. Sweet youth, please, scold me for a whole year together; I'd rather hear you chide than hear this man woo.

12.9.oldText: ROSALIND. He's fallen in love with your foulness, and she'll fall in love with my anger. If so, as fast as she answers you with frowning looks, I'll season her with bitter words. Why do you look so at me?

12.10.oldText: PHEBE. For no ill will I bear you.

12.11.oldText: ROSALIND. Please don't fall in love with me, For I am falser than vows made in wine; Besides, I do not like you. If you want to know where I live, It's at the tuft of olive trees nearby. Will you come, sister? Shepherd, press her hard. Come, sister. Shepherdess, look on him more kindly, And be not proud; though all the world could see, None could be so deceived in sight as he. Come, to our flock. Exeunt ROSALIND, CELIA, and CORIN

12.12.oldText: PHEBE. Dead shepherd, now I find your saying of might: 'Who ever loved that loved not at first sight?'

12.14.oldText: PHEBE. Ha! What do you say, Silvius?

12.16.oldText: PHEBE. Why, I am sorry for you, gentle Silvius.

12.17.oldText: SILVIUS. Wherever sorrow is, relief should be. If you sorrow at my grief in love, By giving love, your sorrow and my grief Would both be ended.

12.18.oldText: PHEBE. You have my love; isn't that neighborly?

12.19.oldText: SILVIUS. I want to have you.

12.20.oldText: PHEBE. Why, that would be covetousness. Silvius, there was a time when I hated you; And yet it is not that I bear you love now; But since you can talk of love so well, Your company, which used to be irksome to me, I will endure; and I'll employ you too. But don't look for further reward Than your own gladness that you're employed.

12.21.oldText: SILVIUS. So holy and so perfect is my love, And I in such a poverty of grace, That I shall think it a most plenteous crop To glean the broken ears of grain behind the man Who reaps the main harvest; if I might gather, now and then, A scattered smile, I would live upon that.

12.22.oldText: PHEBE. Do you know the youth that spoke to me a while ago?

12.23.oldText: SILVIUS. Not very well; but I've met him often; And he has bought the cottage and the lands That the old peasant once was master of.

12.24.oldText: PHEBE. Don't think I love him, though I ask about him; He's only a peevish boy; yet he talks well. But what care I for words? Yet words do well When he that speaks them pleases those who hear. He is a pretty youth—not very pretty; But, sure, he's proud; and yet his pride becomes him. He'll make a proper man. The best thing in him Is his complexion; and faster than his tongue Did offense, his eye healed it up. He's not very tall; yet for his years he's tall; His leg is only so-so; and yet it's well enough. There was a pretty redness in his lip, A little riper and more lusty red Than the red mixed in his cheek; it was just the difference Between the constant red and the mingled damask. There are some women, Silvius—had they marked him In parts as I did—would have come close To falling in love with him; but, for my part, I love him not, nor hate him not; and yet I have more cause to hate him than to love him; For what did he have to do, to chide at me? He said my eyes were black, and my hair black, And, now I remember, scorned at me. I wonder why I didn't answer him back; But that's all one: silence is no surrender. I'll write him a very taunting letter, And you shall carry it; will you, Silvius?

12.25.oldText: SILVIUS. Phebe, with all my heart.

12.26.oldText: PHEBE. I'll write it straight away. The matter's in my head and in my heart; I will be bitter with him, and exceedingly brief. Go with me, Silvius. Exeunt

12.33.oldText: JAQUES. Please, pretty youth, let me become better acquainted with you.

12.34.oldText: ROSALIND. They say you are a melancholy fellow.

12.35.oldText: JAQUES. I am; I like it better than laughing.

12.36.oldText: ROSALIND. Those who are in extremes of either are abominable fellows, and betray themselves to every modern censure worse than drunkards do.

12.37.oldText: JAQUES. Why, it's good to be sad and say nothing.

12.38.oldText: ROSALIND. Why then, it's good to be a fence-post.

12.39.oldText: JAQUES. I have neither the scholar's melancholy, which is rivalry; nor the musician's, which is fantastical; nor the courtier's, which is proud; nor the soldier's, which is ambitious; nor the lawyer's, which is calculating; nor the lady's, which is fastidious; nor the lover's, which is all of these; but it is a melancholy of my own, compounded of many simples, extracted from many objects, and indeed the various contemplation of my travels; in which my frequent rumination wraps me in a most humorous sadness.

12.40.oldText: ROSALIND. A traveler! By my faith, you have great reason to be sad. I fear you've sold your own lands to see other men's; then to have seen much and to have nothing is to have rich eyes and poor hands.

12.41.oldText: JAQUES. Yes, I have gained my experience.

12.43.oldText: ROSALIND. And your experience makes you sad. I'd rather have a fool to make me merry than experience to make me sad—and to travel to get it, too.

12.44.oldText: ORLANDO. Good day, and happiness, dear Rosalind!

12.45.oldText: JAQUES. No, then, God be with you, since you talk in blank verse.

12.46.oldText: ROSALIND. Farewell, Monsieur Traveler; mind you lisp and wear strange suits, disparage all the benefits of your own country, be out of love with your nativity, and almost scold God for making you that face you have; or I'll scarcely believe you have swum in a gondola. [Exit JAQUES] Why, what now, Orlando! Where have you been all this while? You, a lover! If you serve me such another trick, never come into my sight again.

12.47.oldText: ORLANDO. My fair Rosalind, I come within an hour of my promise.

12.48.oldText: ROSALIND. Break an hour's promise in love! He who will divide a minute into a thousand parts, and break only a part of the thousand part of a minute in the affairs of love, it may be said of him that Cupid has clapped him on the shoulder, but I'll guarantee him heart-whole.

12.50.oldText: ROSALIND. No, if you are so tardy, come no more in my sight. I'd just as soon be wooed by a snail.

12.52.oldText: ROSALIND. Yes, by a snail; for though he comes slowly, he carries his house on his head—a better jointure-settlement, I think, than you make for a woman. Besides, he brings his destiny with him.

12.54.oldText: ROSALIND. Why, horns—the kind that men like you are bound to be indebted to your wives for; but he comes armed in his own fortune, and prevents the slander of his wife.

12.55.oldText: ORLANDO. Virtue is no horn-maker; and my Rosalind is virtuous.

12.56.oldText: ROSALIND. And I am your Rosalind.

12.57.oldText: CELIA. It pleases him to call you so; but he has a Rosalind of a better look than you.

12.58.oldText: ROSALIND. Come, woo me, woo me; for now I am in a holiday mood, and likely enough to consent. What would you say to me now, if I were your very, very Rosalind?

12.59.oldText: ORLANDO. I would kiss before I spoke.

12.60.oldText: ROSALIND. No, you'd better speak first; and when you were stuck for lack of matter, you might take occasion to kiss. Very good orators, when they run dry, will spit; and for lovers lacking—God help us!—matter, the cleanliest shift is to kiss.

12.61.oldText: ORLANDO. What if the kiss is denied?

12.62.oldText: ROSALIND. Then she puts you to entreaty, and there begins new matter.

12.63.oldText: ORLANDO. Who could run out of words, being before his beloved mistress?

12.64.oldText: ROSALIND. Marry, you would, if I were your mistress; or I should think my honesty stronger than my wit.

12.65.oldText: ORLANDO. What, out of my suit?

12.66.oldText: ROSALIND. Not out of your apparel, and yet out of your suit. Am I not your Rosalind?

12.67.oldText: ORLANDO. I take some joy in saying you are, because I'd like to be talking of her.

12.68.oldText: ROSALIND. Well, in her person, I say I will not have you.

12.69.oldText: ORLANDO. Then, in my own person, I die.

12.70.oldText: ROSALIND. No, faith, die by proxy. The poor world is almost six thousand years old, and in all that time there was never any man who died in his own person, that is to say, from love. Troilus had his brains dashed out with a Grecian club; yet he did what he could to die before, and he is one of the patterns of love. Leander would have lived many a fair year, even if Hero had turned nun, if it hadn't been for a hot midsummer night; for, good youth, he only went out to wash himself in the Hellespont, and, being seized by a cramp, was drowned; and the foolish chroniclers of that age said it was for love of Hero of Sestos. But these are all lies: men have died from time to time, and worms have eaten them, but not for love.

12.71.oldText: ORLANDO. I wouldn't have my true Rosalind think this way; for I swear, her frown might kill me.

12.72.oldText: ROSALIND. By this hand, it wouldn't kill a fly. But come, now I'll be your Rosalind in a more accommodating mood; and ask me what you will, I'll grant it.

12.74.oldText: ROSALIND. Yes, faith, I will, Fridays and Saturdays, and all.

12.75.oldText: ORLANDO. And will you have me?

12.80.oldText: ROSALIND. Why then, can one desire too much of a good thing? Come, sister, you shall be the priest, and marry us. Give me your hand, Orlando. What do you say, sister?

12.82.oldText: CELIA. I can't say the words.

12.83.oldText: ROSALIND. You must begin 'Will you, Orlando'—

12.84.oldText: CELIA. All right then. Will you, Orlando, take this Rosalind as your wife?

12.87.oldText: ORLANDO. Why, now; as fast as she can marry us.

12.88.oldText: ROSALIND. Then you must say 'I take you, Rosalind, for my wife.'

12.89.oldText: ORLANDO. I take you, Rosalind, for my wife.

12.90.oldText: ROSALIND. I might ask you for your license; but—I do take you, Orlando, for my husband. There's a girl who goes ahead of the priest; and, certainly, a woman's thought runs ahead of her actions.

12.91.oldText: ORLANDO. So do all thoughts; they are winged.

12.92.oldText: ROSALIND. Now tell me how long you would have her, after you have possessed her.

12.94.oldText: ROSALIND. Say 'a day' without the 'forever.' No, no, Orlando; men are April when they woo, December when they wed. Maids are May when they are maids, but the sky changes when they are wives. I will be more jealous of you than a Barbary cock-pigeon over his hen, more clamorous than a parrot against rain, more new-fangled than an ape, more giddy in my desires than a monkey. I will weep for nothing, like Diana in the fountain, and I'll do that when you're disposed to be merry. I'll laugh like a hyena, and that when you're inclined to sleep.

12.95.oldText: ORLANDO. But will my Rosalind do so?

12.96.oldText: ROSALIND. By my life, she will do as I do.

12.97.oldText: ORLANDO. Oh, but she is wise.

12.98.oldText: ROSALIND. Or else she could not have the wit to do this. The wiser, the more wayward. Shut the door upon a woman's wit, and it will go out by the window; shut that, and it will go out at the keyhole; stop that, and it will fly with the smoke out the chimney.

12.99.oldText: ORLANDO. A man who had a wife with such a wit, he might say, 'Wit, where are you going?' ROSALIND. No, you might keep that retort for when you met your wife's wit going to your neighbor's bed.

12.100.oldText: ORLANDO. And what wit could wit have to excuse that?

12.101.oldText: ROSALIND. Marry, to say she came there to look for you. You'll never catch her without an answer, unless you take her without her tongue. Oh, that woman who can't turn her fault into her husband's occasion—let her never nurse her child herself, for she'll raise it like a fool!

12.102.oldText: ORLANDO. For these next two hours, Rosalind, I must leave you.

12.103.oldText: ROSALIND. Alas, dear love, I cannot do without you for two hours!

12.104.oldText: ORLANDO. I must attend the Duke at dinner; by two o'clock I'll be with you again.

12.105.oldText: ROSALIND. Yes, go your ways, go your ways. I knew what you would turn out to be; my friends told me as much, and I thought no less. That flattering tongue of yours won me. It's only one more woman cast away, and so—come death! Two o'clock is your hour?

12.107.oldText: ROSALIND. By my faith, and in good earnest, and so God mend me, and by all pretty oaths that are not dangerous, if you break one jot of your promise, or come one minute behind your hour, I will think you the most pathetical break-promise, and the most hollow lover, and the most unworthy of her you call Rosalind, who may be picked out of the gross band of the unfaithful. So beware my censure, and keep your promise.

12.108.oldText: ORLANDO. With no less religion than if you were indeed my Rosalind; so, adieu.

12.109.oldText: ROSALIND. Well, Time is the old justice who examines all such offenders, and let Time try. Adieu. Exit ORLANDO

12.110.oldText: CELIA. You have simply misused our sex in your love-prate. We must have your doublet and hose pulled over your head, and show the world what the bird has done to her own nest.

12.111.oldText: ROSALIND. Oh cousin, cousin, cousin, my pretty little cousin, if only you knew how many fathoms deep I am in love! But it can't be sounded; my affection has an unknown bottom, like the Bay of Portugal.

12.112.oldText: CELIA. Or rather, bottomless—so that as fast as you pour affection in, it runs out.

12.113.oldText: ROSALIND. No; that same wicked bastard of Venus, who was begotten of thought, conceived of spleen, and born of madness; that blind rascally boy, who abuses everyone's eyes because his own are out—let him be judge how deep I am in love. I'll tell you, Aliena, I cannot be out of the sight of Orlando. I'll go find a shadow, and sigh till he comes.

13.1.oldText: Enter JAQUES and LORDS, in the habit of foresters

13.2.oldText: JAQUES. Which one is he that killed the deer?

13.4.oldText: JAQUES. Let's present him to the Duke, like a Roman conqueror; and it would be fitting to set the deer's horns upon his head as a branch of victory. Have you no song, forester, for this purpose?

13.6.oldText: JAQUES. Sing it; no matter whether it's in tune, so long as it makes noise enough.

13.8.oldText: What shall he have that killed the deer? His leather skin and horns to wear.

13.11.oldText: Take no scorn at wearing the horn; It was a crest before you were born. Your father's father wore it; And your father bore it. The horn, the horn, the lusty horn, Is not a thing to laugh to scorn. Exeunt

14.2.oldText: ROSALIND. What do you say now? Isn't it past two o'clock? And no sign of Orlando!

14.3.oldText: CELIA. I warrant you, with pure love and troubled brain, he has taken his bow and arrows, and gone off—to sleep. Look, who comes here.

14.5.oldText: SILVIUS. My errand is to you, fair youth; My gentle Phebe bade me give you this. I do not know the contents; but, as I guess By the stern brow and waspish manner She had as she was writing it, It carries an angry tone. Pardon me, I am only a guiltless messenger.

14.6.oldText: ROSALIND. Patience herself would startle at this letter, And play the swaggerer. Bear this, bear all. She says I am not fair, that I lack manners; She calls me proud, and says she could not love me, Were a man as rare as a Phoenix. By my will! Her love is not the hare I am hunting; Why does she write to me like this? Well, shepherd, well, This is a letter of your own contrivance.

14.7.oldText: SILVIUS. No, I protest, I do not know the contents; Phebe did write it.

14.8.oldText: ROSALIND. Come, come, you are a fool, And turned to the extremity of love. I saw her hand; she has a leathern hand, A freestone-colored hand; I really did think Her old gloves were on, but it was her hands; She has a housewife's hand—but that's no matter. I tell you, she never invented this letter: This is a man's invention, and a man's handwriting.

14.10.oldText: ROSALIND. Why, it's a boisterous and a cruel style; A style for challengers. Why, she defies me, Like Turk to Christian. Women's gentle brain Could not produce such giant-rude invention, Such Ethiope words, blacker in their meaning Than in their appearance. Will you hear the letter?

14.11.oldText: SILVIUS. If you please, for I have not heard it yet; Though I have heard too much of Phebe's cruelty.

14.12.oldText: ROSALIND. She Phebes me: mark how the tyrant writes.

14.14.oldText: 'Are you a god turned shepherd, That a maiden's heart has burned?'

14.15.oldText: Can a woman rail like this?

14.17.oldText: ROSALIND. 'Why, with your godhead laid aside, Do you war with a woman's heart?'

14.18.oldText: Did you ever hear such railing?

14.19.oldText: 'While the eye of man did woo me, That could do no harm to me.'

14.21.oldText: 'If the scorn of your bright eyes Have power to raise such love in mine, Alas, in me what strange effect Would they work in mild aspect! While you scolded me, I did love; How then might your prayers move me! He that brings this love to you Little knows this love in me; And by him seal up your answer, Whether your youth and kind Will take the faithful offer Of me and all that I can make; Or else by him my love deny, And then I'll study how to die.'

14.24.oldText: ROSALIND. Do you pity him? No, he deserves no pity. Will you love such a woman? What, to make you an instrument and play false notes upon you! Not to be endured! Well, go your way back to her, since I see love has made you a tame snake, and tell her this—that if she loves me, I command her to love you; if she will not, I will never have her, unless you plead for her. If you're a true lover, go—and not a word; for here comes more company. Exit SILVIUS

14.26.oldText: OLIVER. Good morning, fair ones; please, if you know, Where in the outskirts of this forest stands A sheep-cote fenced about with olive trees?

14.27.oldText: CELIA. West of this place, down in the neighboring valley. The row of willows by the murmuring stream, Left on your right hand, brings you to the place. But at this hour the house is empty; There's no one inside.

14.28.oldText: OLIVER. If an eye may profit by a tongue, Then I should know you by description— Such garments, and such years: 'The boy is fair, Of female features, and conducts himself Like a grown sister; the woman is short, And browner than her brother.' Are you not The owners of the house I was asking after?

14.29.oldText: CELIA. It's no boast, when asked, to say we are.

14.30.oldText: OLIVER. Orlando commends himself to you both; And to that youth he calls his Rosalind He sends this bloody handkerchief. Are you he?

14.31.oldText: ROSALIND. I am. What must we understand by this?

14.32.oldText: OLIVER. Something of my shame, if you will hear from me What man I am, and how, and why, and where, This handkerchief was stained.

14.34.oldText: OLIVER. When last young Orlando parted from you, He left a promise to return Within an hour; and, walking through the forest, Chewing on the food of sweet and bitter fancy, Lo, what happened! He cast his eye aside, And mark what object appeared. Under an oak, whose boughs were mossed with age, And high top bald with dry antiquity, A wretched ragged man, overgrown with hair, Lay sleeping on his back. About his neck A green and gilded snake had wreathed itself, Who with her head, nimble in threats, approached The opening of his mouth; but suddenly, Seeing Orlando, it unwound itself, And with zigzag glides slipped away Into a bush; under whose shade A lioness, with udders all drawn dry, Lay crouching, head on the ground, with catlike watch, Waiting for the sleeping man to stir; for it's The royal disposition of that beast To prey on nothing that seems already dead. Seeing this, Orlando did approach the man, And found it was his brother, his elder brother.

14.35.oldText: CELIA. Oh, I have heard him speak of that very brother; And he described him as the most unnatural Who lived among men.

14.36.oldText: OLIVER. And well he might do so, For well I know he was unnatural.

14.37.oldText: ROSALIND. But, of Orlando: did he leave him there, Food for the sucked-dry and hungry lioness?

14.38.oldText: OLIVER. Twice he turned his back, and meant to do so; But kindness, nobler always than revenge, And nature, stronger than his just provocation, Made him give battle to the lioness, Who quickly fell before him; in which struggle From miserable slumber I awoke.

14.40.oldText: ROSALIND. Was it you he rescued?

14.41.oldText: CELIA. Was it you who so often contrived to kill him?

14.42.oldText: OLIVER. It was I; but it is not I now. I am not ashamed To tell you what I was, since my conversion Tastes so sweetly, being the thing I am now.

14.43.oldText: ROSALIND. But what about the bloody handkerchief?

14.44.oldText: OLIVER. In a moment. When from the first to last, between us two, Tears had most kindly bathed our accounts— Such as how I came to that desert place— In brief, he led me to the gentle Duke, Who gave me fresh clothes and entertainment, Committing me to my brother's love. He led me instantly to his cave, There stripped himself, and here upon his arm The lioness had torn away some flesh, Which all this while had bled; and now he fainted, And cried, in fainting, upon Rosalind. Briefly, I revived him, bound up his wound, And, after some short time, being strong at heart, He sent me here, stranger as I am, To tell this story, so that you might excuse His broken promise, and to give this handkerchief, Dyed in his blood, to the shepherd youth Whom he in sport calls his Rosalind.

14.46.oldText: CELIA. Why, what now, Ganymede! Sweet Ganymede!

14.47.oldText: OLIVER. Many will swoon when they look on blood.

14.48.oldText: CELIA. There's more to it. Cousin Ganymede!

14.50.oldText: ROSALIND. I wish I were at home.

14.51.oldText: CELIA. We'll lead you there. Please, will you take him by the arm?

14.52.oldText: OLIVER. Be of good cheer, youth. You, a man! You lack a man's heart.

14.53.oldText: ROSALIND. I do, I confess it. Ah, sir, anybody would think this was well counterfeited. Please tell your brother how well I counterfeited. Heigh-ho!

14.54.oldText: OLIVER. This was not counterfeit; there's too great a witness in your complexion that it was a passion in earnest.

14.56.oldText: OLIVER. Well then, take heart and counterfeit to be a man.

14.57.oldText: ROSALIND. So I do; but, in faith, I should have been a woman by right.

14.58.oldText: CELIA. Come, you look paler and paler; please, head for home. Good sir, come with us.

14.59.oldText: OLIVER. That I will, for I must carry back word How you excuse my brother, Rosalind.

14.60.oldText: ROSALIND. I shall devise something; but please, commend my counterfeiting to him. Will you come? Exeunt

14.67.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. We shall find a time, Audrey; patience, gentle Audrey.

14.68.oldText: AUDREY. Faith, the priest was good enough, for all that the old gentleman said.

14.69.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. A most wicked Sir Oliver, Audrey, a most vile Martext. But, Audrey, there's a youth here in the forest who lays claim to you.

14.70.oldText: AUDREY. Yes, I know who it is; he has no claim on me in the world; here comes the man you mean.

14.72.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. It's meat and drink to me to see a clown. By my faith, we who have good wits have much to answer for: we shall be flouting; we can't hold back.

14.74.oldText: AUDREY. God give you good evening, William.

14.75.oldText: WILLIAM. And good evening to you, sir.

14.76.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. Good evening, gentle friend. Cover your head, cover your head; no, please, put your hat back on. How old are you, friend?

14.78.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. A ripe age. Is your name William?

14.80.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. A fair name. Were you born in this forest?

14.81.oldText: WILLIAM. Yes, sir, I thank God.

14.82.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. 'Thank God.' A good answer. Are you rich?

14.84.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. 'So-so' is good, very good, very excellently good; and yet it is not; it is only so-so. Are you wise?

14.85.oldText: WILLIAM. Yes, sir, I have a pretty wit.

14.86.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. Why, you say well. I now remember a saying: 'The fool thinks he is wise, but the wise man knows himself to be a fool.' The heathen philosopher, when he had a desire to eat a grape, would open his lips when he put it into his mouth; meaning thereby that grapes were made to be eaten and lips to be opened. Do you love this maid?

14.88.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. Give me your hand. Are you learned?

14.90.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. Then learn this from me: to have is to have; for it is a figure in rhetoric that drink, being poured out of a cup into a glass, by filling the one empties the other; for all your writers agree that ipse is he; now, you are not ipse, for I am he.

14.92.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. He, sir, who must marry this woman. Therefore, you clown, abandon—which in the vulgar tongue means leave—the society—which in boorish speech means company—of this female—which in common speech means woman—which all together comes to: abandon the society of this female; or, clown, you perish; or, in plainer words, you die; or, to wit, I kill you, do away with you, translate your life into death, your liberty into bondage. I will deal with you in poison, or in cudgeling, or in steel; I will scheme with you in faction; I will overrun you with policy; I will kill you a hundred and fifty ways; therefore tremble and depart.

14.94.oldText: WILLIAM. God rest you merry, sir. Exit

14.96.oldText: CORIN. Our master and mistress are looking for you; come away, away.

14.97.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. Trip, Audrey, trip, Audrey. I'm coming, I'm coming. Exeunt

15.2.oldText: ORLANDO. Is it possible that on so little acquaintance you should like her? That just by seeing her you should love her? And, loving, woo her? And, wooing, she should accept? And do you persevere in wanting to enjoy her?

15.3.oldText: OLIVER. Don't call the giddiness of it into question, nor her poverty, nor our small acquaintance, nor my sudden wooing, nor her sudden consenting; but say with me, I love Aliena; say with her that she loves me; consent with both of us that we may enjoy each other. It shall be to your good; for my father's house and all the income that was old Sir Rowland's I'll settle on you, and here live and die a shepherd.

15.4.oldText: ORLANDO. You have my consent. Let your wedding be tomorrow. I'll invite the Duke and all his contented followers. Go and prepare Aliena; for, look you, here comes my Rosalind.

15.7.oldText: OLIVER. And you, fair sister. Exit

15.8.oldText: ROSALIND. Oh, my dear Orlando, how it grieves me to see you wear your heart in a scarf!

15.10.oldText: ROSALIND. I thought your heart had been wounded by the claws of a lion.

15.11.oldText: ORLANDO. Wounded it is, but with the eyes of a lady.

15.12.oldText: ROSALIND. Did your brother tell you how I counterfeited a swoon when he showed me your handkerchief?

15.13.oldText: ORLANDO. Yes, and greater wonders than that.

15.14.oldText: ROSALIND. Oh, I know what you're getting at. No, it's true. There was never anything so sudden but the fight of two rams and Caesar's boastful brag of 'I came, saw, and overcame.' For your brother and my sister no sooner met than they looked; no sooner looked than they loved; no sooner loved than they sighed; no sooner sighed than they asked one another the reason; no sooner knew the reason than they sought the remedy—and by these degrees they have made a pair of stairs to marriage, which they will climb without delay, or else be without restraint before marriage. They are in the very fury of

15.15.oldText: love, and they will be together. Clubs cannot part them.

15.16.oldText: ORLANDO. They shall be married tomorrow; and I will invite the Duke to the wedding. But, oh, how bitter a thing it is to look into happiness through another man's eyes! By how much the more shall I tomorrow be at the height of heart-heaviness, by how much I shall think my brother happy in having what he wishes for.

15.17.oldText: ROSALIND. Why then, tomorrow I cannot serve your turn for Rosalind?

15.18.oldText: ORLANDO. I can live no longer by thinking.

15.19.oldText: ROSALIND. I'll weary you, then, no longer with idle talk. Know this from me then—for now I speak to some purpose—that I know you are a gentleman of good understanding. I'm not saying this so you'll have a good opinion of my knowledge, insofar as I say I know you are; nor do I labor for a greater esteem than may in some little measure draw a belief from you, to do yourself good, and not to grace me. Believe then, if you please, that I can do strange things. I have, since I was three years old, conversed with a magician, most profound in his art and yet not damnable. If you love Rosalind as near the heart as your gestures cry it out, when your brother marries Aliena, you shall marry her. I know into what straits of fortune she's been driven; and it's not impossible for me—if it doesn't seem inconvenient to you—to set her before your eyes tomorrow, human as she is, and without any danger.

15.20.oldText: ORLANDO. Are you speaking with sober meaning?

15.21.oldText: ROSALIND. By my life, I am; which I value dearly, even though I say I'm a magician. So put on your best clothes, invite your friends; for if you want to be married tomorrow, you shall; and to Rosalind, if you will.

15.23.oldText: Look, here comes a lover of mine, and a lover of hers.

15.24.oldText: PHEBE. Youth, you have done me much ungentleness By showing the letter that I wrote to you.

15.25.oldText: ROSALIND. I don't care if I have. It is my study To seem despiteful and ungentle to you. You are followed there by a faithful shepherd; Look upon him, love him; he worships you.

15.26.oldText: PHEBE. Good shepherd, tell this youth what it is to love.

15.27.oldText: SILVIUS. It is to be all made of sighs and tears; And so am I for Phebe.

15.30.oldText: ROSALIND. And I for no woman.

15.31.oldText: SILVIUS. It is to be all made of faith and service; And so am I for Phebe.

15.34.oldText: ROSALIND. And I for no woman.

15.35.oldText: SILVIUS. It is to be all made of fantasy, All made of passion, and all made of wishes; All adoration, duty, and observance, All humbleness, all patience, and impatience, All purity, all trial, all obedience; And so am I for Phebe.

15.36.oldText: PHEBE. And so am I for Ganymede.

15.37.oldText: ORLANDO. And so am I for Rosalind.

15.38.oldText: ROSALIND. And so am I for no woman.

15.39.oldText: PHEBE. If this is so, why blame me for loving you?

15.40.oldText: SILVIUS. If this is so, why blame me for loving you?

15.41.oldText: ORLANDO. If this is so, why blame me for loving you?

15.42.oldText: ROSALIND. Why are you saying it too: 'Why blame me for loving you?'

15.43.oldText: ORLANDO. To her who is not here, nor does not hear.

15.44.oldText: ROSALIND. Please, no more of this; it's like the howling of Irish wolves against the moon. [To SILVIUS] I will help you if I can.

15.45.oldText: [To PHEBE] I would love you if I could.—Tomorrow meet me

15.46.oldText: all together. [To PHEBE] I will marry you if ever I marry a woman, and I'll be married tomorrow. [To ORLANDO] I will satisfy you if ever I satisfied a man, and you shall be married tomorrow. [To SILVIUS] I will content you if what pleases you contents you, and you shall be married tomorrow. [To ORLANDO] As you love Rosalind, meet. [To SILVIUS] As you love Phebe, meet;—and as I love no woman, I'll meet. So, fare you well; I've left you with your orders.

15.47.oldText: SILVIUS. I'll not fail, if I live.

16.2.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. Tomorrow is the joyful day, Audrey; tomorrow we shall be married.

16.3.oldText: AUDREY. I do desire it with all my heart; and I hope it is no dishonest desire to wish to be a woman of the world. Here come two of the banished Duke's pages.

16.5.oldText: FIRST PAGE. Well met, honest gentleman.

16.6.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. By my faith, well met. Come, sit, sit, and a song.

16.7.oldText: SECOND PAGE. We're at your service; sit in the middle.

16.8.oldText: FIRST PAGE. Shall we plunge right into it, without hawking, or spitting, or saying we're hoarse, which are the only prologues to a bad voice?

16.9.oldText: SECOND PAGE. In faith, in faith; and both in tune, like two gypsies on one horse.

16.10.oldText: SONG. It was a lover and his lass, With a hey, and a ho, and a hey nonino, That over the green cornfield did pass In the spring time, the only pretty ring time, When birds do sing, hey ding a ding, ding. Sweet lovers love the spring.

16.11.oldText: Between the acres of the rye, With a hey, and a ho, and a hey nonino, These pretty country folks would lie, In the spring time, &c.

16.12.oldText: This carol they began that hour, With a hey, and a ho, and a hey nonino, How that a life was but a flower, In the spring time, &c.

16.13.oldText: And therefore take the present time, With a hey, and a ho, and a hey nonino, For love is crowned with the prime, In the spring time, &c.

16.14.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. Truly, young gentlemen, though there was no great matter in the ditty, yet the tune was very out of key.

16.15.oldText: FIRST PAGE. You're mistaken, sir; we kept time, we did not lose our time.

16.16.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. By my faith, yes; I count it only time lost to hear such a foolish song. God be with you; and God mend your voices. Come, Audrey. Exeunt

17.1.oldText: Enter DUKE SENIOR, AMIENS, JAQUES, ORLANDO, OLIVER, and CELIA

17.2.oldText: DUKE SENIOR. Do you believe, Orlando, that the boy Can do all this that he has promised?

17.3.oldText: ORLANDO. I sometimes believe and sometimes do not: Like those who fear what they hope, and know they fear.

17.5.oldText: ROSALIND. Patience once more, while our compact is laid out: You say, if I bring in your Rosalind, You will bestow her on Orlando here?

17.6.oldText: DUKE SENIOR. That I would, had I kingdoms to give with her.

17.7.oldText: ROSALIND. And you say you will have her when I bring her?

17.8.oldText: ORLANDO. That I would, were I king of all kingdoms.

17.9.oldText: ROSALIND. You say you'll marry me, if I am willing?

17.10.oldText: PHEBE. That I will, even if I die the hour after.

17.11.oldText: ROSALIND. But if you do refuse to marry me, You'll give yourself to this most faithful shepherd?

17.13.oldText: ROSALIND. You say that you'll have Phebe, if she will?

17.14.oldText: SILVIUS. Even if to have her and death were both one thing.

17.15.oldText: ROSALIND. I have promised to make all this matter even. Keep your word, O Duke, to give your daughter; You yours, Orlando, to receive his daughter; Keep your word, Phebe, that you'll marry me, Or else, refusing me, will wed this shepherd; Keep your word, Silvius, that you'll marry her If she refuses me; and from here I go, To make these doubts all even. Exeunt ROSALIND and CELIA

17.16.oldText: DUKE SENIOR. I do recognize in this shepherd boy Some lively touches of my daughter's features.

17.17.oldText: ORLANDO. My lord, the first time that I ever saw him I thought he was a brother to your daughter. But, my good lord, this boy is forest-born, And has been tutored in the rudiments Of many desperate studies by his uncle, Whom he reports to be a great magician, Hidden in the circle of this forest.

17.19.oldText: JAQUES. There is, surely, another flood coming, and these couples are coming to the ark. Here comes a pair of very strange beasts which in all tongues are called fools.

17.20.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. Salutation and greeting to you all!

17.21.oldText: JAQUES. My good lord, bid him welcome. This is the motley-minded gentleman that I have so often met in the forest. He has been a courtier, he swears.

17.22.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. If anyone doubts that, let him put me to my purgation. I have trod a measure; I have flattered a lady; I have been politic with my friend, smooth with my enemy; I have ruined three tailors; I have had four quarrels, and was likely to have fought one.

17.23.oldText: JAQUES. And how was that one settled?

17.24.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. Faith, we met, and found the quarrel was upon the seventh cause.

17.25.oldText: JAQUES. How, seventh cause? My good lord, like this fellow.

17.26.oldText: DUKE SENIOR. I like him very well.

17.27.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. God reward you, sir; I wish the same for you. I press in here, sir, among the rest of the country couplers, to swear and to forswear, according as marriage binds and blood breaks. A poor virgin, sir, an ill-favored thing, sir, but my own; a poor humor of mine, sir, to take what other men would refuse. Rich honesty dwells, like a miser, sir, in a poor house; just as your pearl in your foul oyster.

17.28.oldText: DUKE SENIOR. By my faith, he is very swift and sententious.

17.29.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. After the fashion of the fool's quick bolt, sir, and such sweet diseases.

17.30.oldText: JAQUES. But, about the seventh cause: how did you find the quarrel was on the seventh cause?

17.31.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. Upon a lie seven times removed—carry yourself more becomingly, Audrey—as thus, sir. I disliked the cut of a certain courtier's beard. He sent me word that, if I said his beard was not cut well, he was of the mind that it was. This is called the Retort Courteous. If I sent him word again that it was not well cut, he would send word that he cut it to please himself. This is called the Quip Modest. If again that it was not well cut, he disparaged my judgment. This is called the Reply Churlish. If again it was not well cut, he would answer I did not speak the truth. This is called the Reproof Valiant. If again it was not well cut, he would say I lie. This is called the Countercheck Quarrelsome. And so on to the Lie Circumstantial and the Lie Direct.

17.32.oldText: JAQUES. And how often did you say his beard was not well cut?

17.33.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. I dared go no further than the Lie Circumstantial, nor did he dare give me the Lie Direct; and so we measured swords and parted.

17.34.oldText: JAQUES. Can you name in order now the degrees of the lie?

17.35.oldText: TOUCHSTONE. Oh, sir, we quarrel by the book, just as you have books for good manners. I will name you the degrees. The first, the Retort Courteous; the second, the Quip Modest; the third, the Reply Churlish; the fourth, the Reproof Valiant; the fifth, the Countercheck Quarrelsome; the sixth, the Lie with Circumstance; the seventh, the Lie Direct. All these you may avoid except the Lie Direct; and you may avoid that too with an If. I knew when seven justices could not settle a quarrel; but when the parties met themselves, one of them thought only of an If, as: 'If you

17.36.oldText: said so, then I said so.' And they shook hands, and swore brotherhood. Your If is the only peacemaker; much virtue in If.

17.37.oldText: JAQUES. Is not this a rare fellow, my lord? He's as good at anything, and yet a fool.

17.38.oldText: DUKE SENIOR. He uses his folly like a stalking-horse, and under the cover of it he shoots his wit.

17.39.oldText: Enter HYMEN, ROSALIND, and CELIA. Still MUSIC

17.40.oldText: HYMEN. Then there is mirth in heaven, When earthly things, made even, Are reconciled together. Good Duke, receive your daughter; Hymen from heaven has brought her, Yes, brought her hither, That you might join her hand with his Whose heart is within his bosom.

17.41.oldText: ROSALIND. [To DUKE] To you I give myself, for I am yours.

17.42.oldText: [To ORLANDO] To you I give myself, for I am yours.

17.43.oldText: DUKE SENIOR. If there be truth in sight, you are my daughter.

17.44.oldText: ORLANDO. If there be truth in sight, you are my Rosalind.

17.45.oldText: PHEBE. If sight and shape be true, Why then, my love adieu!

17.46.oldText: ROSALIND. I'll have no father, if you are not he; I'll have no husband, if you are not he; Nor ever wed any woman, if you are not she.

17.47.oldText: HYMEN. Peace, ho! I bar confusion; It is I must make the conclusion Of these most strange events. Here are eight that must take hands To join in Hymen's bands, If truth holds true contents. You and you no cross shall part; You and you are heart to heart; You to his love must accord, Or have a woman as your lord; You and you are sure together, As the winter to foul weather. While a wedlock-hymn we sing, Feed yourselves with questioning, That reason wonder may diminish— How we thus met, and these things finish.

17.48.oldText: SONG Wedding is great Juno's crown; O blessed bond of board and bed! It is Hymen who peoples every town; High wedlock then be honored. Honor, high honor, and renown, To Hymen, god of every town!

17.49.oldText: DUKE SENIOR. O my dear niece, welcome you are to me! Even as daughter, welcome in no less degree.

17.50.oldText: PHEBE. I will not eat my word, now you are mine; Your faith binds my fancy to you.

17.52.oldText: JAQUES de BOYS. Give me audience for a word or two. I am the second son of old Sir Rowland, Who brings these tidings to this fair assembly. Duke Frederick, hearing how every day Men of great worth resorted to this forest, Mustered a mighty force, which were on foot, Under his own command, purposely to capture His brother here, and put him to the sword. And to the edge of this wild wood he came, Where, meeting with an old religious man, After some conversation with him, was converted Both from his enterprise and from the world; His crown bequeathing to his banished brother, And all their lands restored again to those That were exiled with him. This to be true I do pledge my life.

17.53.oldText: DUKE SENIOR. Welcome, young man. You offer a fair gift to your brothers' wedding: To one, his lands withheld; and to the other, A land itself at large, a potent dukedom. First, in this forest let us complete those ends That here were well begun and well begotten; And after, every one of this happy number That has endured rough days and nights with us Shall share the good of our returned fortune, According to the measure of their stations. For now, forget this new-fallen dignity, And fall into our rustic revelry. Play, music; and you brides and bridegrooms all, With measure heaped in joy, to the measures fall.

17.54.oldText: JAQUES. Sir, by your leave. If I heard you rightly, The Duke has put on a religious life, And cast off into neglect the pompous court.

17.56.oldText: JAQUES. Then to him I will go. From these converts There is much matter to be heard and learned.

17.57.oldText: [To DUKE] You to your former honor I bequeath;

17.58.oldText: Your patience and your virtue well deserve it.

17.59.oldText: [To ORLANDO] You to a love that your true faith merits;

17.60.oldText: [To OLIVER] You to your land, and love, and great allies;

17.61.oldText: [To SILVIUS] You to a long and well-deserved bed;

17.62.oldText: [To TOUCHSTONE] And you to wrangling; for your loving voyage

17.63.oldText: Is provisioned for only two months.—So to your pleasures; I am for other things than dancing measures.

17.65.oldText: JAQUES. No pastime for me to see. What you would have, I'll wait to hear at your abandoned cave. Exit

17.66.oldText: DUKE SENIOR. Proceed, proceed. We will begin these rites, As we trust they will end, in true delights. [A dance] Exeunt

17.69.oldText: ROSALIND. It is not the fashion to see the lady give the epilogue; but it is no more unhandsome than to see the lord give the prologue. If it is true that good wine needs no bush, it is true that a good play needs no epilogue. Yet for good wine they do use good bushes; and good plays prove the better by the help of good epilogues. What a fix am I in then, being neither a good epilogue, nor able to insinuate with you on behalf of a good play! I am not dressed like a beggar; therefore to beg will not become me. My way is to conjure you; and I'll begin with the women. I charge you, O women, by the love you bear to men, to like as much of this play as pleases you; and I charge you, O men, by the love you bear to women—as I perceive by your simpering that none of you hates them—that between you and the women the play may please. If I were a woman, I would kiss as many of you as had beards that pleased me, complexions that I liked, and breaths that I did not defy; and, I am sure, as many as have good beards, or good faces, or sweet breaths, will, for my kind offer, when I make my curtsy, bid me farewell.
